Physics I (8.01) - Exercises

Introduction

Units

Derived Units

Use SI units to check whether a physical expression can be meaningful.

Check the unit of kinetic energy

K=\frac12mv^2

Since

[m]=\mathrm{kg}, \qquad [v]=\mathrm{m/s},

the unit is

[K]=\mathrm{kg}\cdot\frac{\mathrm m^2}{\mathrm s^2}

This is the joule:

1\ \mathrm J=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s^2}

Unit checks can reject impossible formulas, but they cannot determine dimensionless constants such as 1/2.

Dimensional Analysis

Use dimensions when the relevant variables are known but the exact dimensionless constant is not.

Assume the free-fall time from height h under gravity g has form

t\propto h^\beta g^\gamma

The dimensions are

[t]=T, \qquad [h]=L, \qquad [g]=LT^{-2}

Thus

T=L^\beta(LT^{-2})^\gamma =L^{\beta+\gamma}T^{-2\gamma}

Match powers of L and T:

\beta+\gamma=0, \qquad -2\gamma=1

So

\gamma=-\frac12, \qquad \beta=\frac12,

and

t\propto\sqrt{\frac hg}

Mass cannot affect the answer here because no mass dimension appears in h, g, or t.

Measurement

Worst-case propagation

Use absolute uncertainties for addition and subtraction, and relative uncertainties for multiplication and division.

Let

x=(2.0\pm0.1)\ \mathrm m, \qquad y=(3.0\pm0.2)\ \mathrm m

For

w=x+y,

the central value and absolute uncertainty are

w=5.0\ \mathrm m, \qquad \Delta w=0.1\ \mathrm m+0.2\ \mathrm m=0.3\ \mathrm m

For

z=xy,

the central value is 6.0\ \mathrm{m^2}, and

\frac{\Delta z}{|z|} =\frac{0.1}{2.0}+\frac{0.2}{3.0} =\frac7{60}

Therefore

\Delta z=6.0\cdot\frac7{60}=0.7\ \mathrm{m^2},

so

z=(6.0\pm0.7)\ \mathrm{m^2}

Choose the uncertainty rule from the operation before simplifying the arithmetic.

Covariance-aware propagation

Use derivative-based propagation when uncertainties are statistical or the measured inputs are correlated.

The sides of a rectangle are measured as

x=(2.0\pm0.1)\ \mathrm m, \qquad y=(3.0\pm0.2)\ \mathrm m,

with

\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)=0.010\ \mathrm{m^2}

Find the uncertainty in its area A=xy. Since

\frac{\partial A}{\partial x}=y, \qquad \frac{\partial A}{\partial y}=x,

the propagated variance is

\begin{aligned} (\Delta A)^2 &=y^2(\Delta x)^2+x^2(\Delta y)^2 +2xy\operatorname{Cov}(x,y) \\ &=3.0^2(0.1)^2+2.0^2(0.2)^2 +2(2.0)(3.0)(0.010) \\ &=0.37\ \mathrm{m^4}. \end{aligned}

Therefore,

A=6.0\ \mathrm{m^2}, \qquad \Delta A=\sqrt{0.37}\approx0.61\ \mathrm{m^2}

Thus

\boxed{A=(6.0\pm0.6)\ \mathrm{m^2}}

If the measurements were independent, the covariance term would vanish and the uncertainty would be 0.50\ \mathrm{m^2}. Positive covariance increases the combined uncertainty here.

Kinematics and Dynamics

Position, Velocity, Acceleration

One-dimensional motion

Use derivatives to move from position to velocity and acceleration; speed is the magnitude of velocity.

For one-dimensional motion,

x(t)=t^3-3t^2+2,

find velocity, acceleration, and speed at t=1.

Differentiate:

v(t)=\frac{dx}{dt}=3t^2-6t, \qquad a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}=6t-6

At t=1,

v(1)=-3, \qquad a(1)=0

The velocity is negative because the particle is moving in the negative x direction, but the speed is non-negative:

|v(1)|=3

Component derivatives

Differentiate each component separately, then use vector magnitude when the problem asks for speed.

Let

\vec r(t)=t^2\hat i+\sin t\hat j+e^t\hat k

Find \vec v(0), \vec a(0), and the speed at t=0.

Differentiate component by component:

\vec v(t)=2t\hat i+\cos t\hat j+e^t\hat k, \qquad \vec a(t)=2\hat i-\sin t\hat j+e^t\hat k

At t=0,

\vec v(0)=\hat j+\hat k, \qquad \vec a(0)=2\hat i+\hat k

The speed is

|\vec v(0)|=\sqrt{0^2+1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2

Circular motion

A particle moves counterclockwise on a circle of radius R=2 in the xy-plane. Its angular position is

\theta(t)=t^2

Find its velocity, speed, and acceleration at t=1. The geometry is defined in Figure 1.

Use

\omega=\dot\theta, \qquad \alpha=\ddot\theta

Figure 2 separates the radial and tangential components used in the solution.

cartesian components

Start from fixed \hat i,\hat j components:

\vec r=R\cos\theta\hat i+R\sin\theta\hat j

Differentiate once:

\begin{aligned} \vec v &=\frac{d\vec r}{dt} \\ &=-R\dot\theta\sin\theta\hat i+R\dot\theta\cos\theta\hat j \\ &=R\omega(-\sin\theta\hat i+\cos\theta\hat j). \end{aligned}

Thus

|\vec v|=R|\omega|

Differentiate each component again:

\begin{aligned} a_x &=\frac{d}{dt}(-R\dot\theta\sin\theta) \\ &=-R\ddot\theta\sin\theta-R\dot\theta^2\cos\theta, \\ a_y &=\frac{d}{dt}(R\dot\theta\cos\theta) \\ &=R\ddot\theta\cos\theta-R\dot\theta^2\sin\theta. \end{aligned}

So

\begin{aligned} \vec a &=(-R\ddot\theta\sin\theta-R\dot\theta^2\cos\theta)\hat i +(R\ddot\theta\cos\theta-R\dot\theta^2\sin\theta)\hat j \\ &=-R\omega^2(\cos\theta\hat i+\sin\theta\hat j) +R\alpha(-\sin\theta\hat i+\cos\theta\hat j). \end{aligned}

With

\hat r=\cos\theta\hat i+\sin\theta\hat j, \qquad \hat\theta=-\sin\theta\hat i+\cos\theta\hat j,

this becomes

\boxed{\vec v=R\omega\hat\theta}, \qquad \boxed{\vec a=-R\omega^2\hat r+R\alpha\hat\theta}

moving unit vectors

For circular motion with fixed radius, write the position as

\vec r=R\hat r, \qquad \hat r=\cos\theta\hat i+\sin\theta\hat j, \qquad \hat\theta=-\sin\theta\hat i+\cos\theta\hat j

The unit vectors change direction as the particle moves. Differentiate the definitions:

\begin{aligned} \frac{d\hat r}{dt} &=\frac{d}{dt}(\cos\theta\hat i+\sin\theta\hat j) \\ &=-\dot\theta\sin\theta\hat i+\dot\theta\cos\theta\hat j \\ &=\dot\theta\hat\theta, \\ \frac{d\hat\theta}{dt} &=\frac{d}{dt}(-\sin\theta\hat i+\cos\theta\hat j) \\ &=-\dot\theta\cos\theta\hat i-\dot\theta\sin\theta\hat j \\ &=-\dot\theta\hat r. \end{aligned}

Now differentiate the position. Since R is constant,

\begin{aligned} \vec v &=\frac{d}{dt}(R\hat r) \\ &=R\frac{d\hat r}{dt} \\ &=R\dot\theta\hat\theta \\ &=R\omega\hat\theta. \end{aligned}

The speed is therefore

|\vec v|=R|\omega|

Differentiate the velocity once more:

\begin{aligned} \vec a &=\frac{d}{dt}(R\omega\hat\theta) \\ &=R\dot\omega\hat\theta+R\omega\frac{d\hat\theta}{dt} \\ &=R\alpha\hat\theta+R\omega(-\dot\theta\hat r) \\ &=R\alpha\hat\theta-R\omega^2\hat r. \end{aligned}

Thus

\boxed{\vec v=R\omega\hat\theta}, \qquad \boxed{\vec a=-R\omega^2\hat r+R\alpha\hat\theta}

Both methods give the same formulas. Now substitute R=2 and t=1:

\theta=1, \qquad \omega=2, \qquad \alpha=2

Therefore

\vec v(1)=4\hat\theta =4(-\sin1\hat i+\cos1\hat j), \qquad |\vec v(1)|=4

The acceleration has a radial part and a tangential part:

\vec a(1)=-8\hat r+4\hat\theta

In fixed \hat i,\hat j components,

\vec a(1) =-8(\cos1\hat i+\sin1\hat j) +4(-\sin1\hat i+\cos1\hat j)

The radial term points inward and changes the direction of velocity; the tangential term changes the speed.

The Laws of Motion

Start from a free-body diagram, choose signs before writing equations, and let the force equations decide whether the assumed motion is possible.

Traffic light held by two cables

A traffic light of mass m hangs from two cables. The cables meet at the light and form a right angle. Let the left cable make angle \alpha above the horizontal, so the right cable makes angle 90^\circ-\alpha above the horizontal, as defined in Figure 3.

At rest, the net force is zero. The forces acting at the light are isolated in Figure 4.

If T_1 is the left-cable tension and T_2 is the right-cable tension, then

\begin{cases} -T_1\cos\alpha+T_2\cos(90^\circ-\alpha)=0,\\ T_1\sin\alpha+T_2\sin(90^\circ-\alpha)-mg=0. \end{cases}

Using \cos(90^\circ-\alpha)=\sin\alpha and \sin(90^\circ-\alpha)=\cos\alpha,

T_2\sin\alpha=T_1\cos\alpha, \qquad T_1\sin\alpha+T_2\cos\alpha=mg

Substitute T_2=T_1\cot\alpha:

T_1\left(\sin\alpha+\frac{\cos^2\alpha}{\sin\alpha}\right)=mg, \qquad T_1=mg\sin\alpha

Therefore

\boxed{T_1=mg\sin\alpha}, \qquad \boxed{T_2=mg\cos\alpha}

If the two cables are symmetric, \alpha=45^\circ, and both tensions are mg/\sqrt2.

Blocks connected by a pulley

A block of mass m_1 hangs vertically. A block of mass m_2 lies on an incline of angle \theta with friction coefficient \mu. The two blocks are connected by a light rope over a frictionless pulley as in Figure 5.

Take positive motion to mean m_1 moves downward and m_2 moves up the incline, using the force and sign conventions in Figure 6. Draw f down the incline; a negative value means that the actual friction points up the incline.

If the system is at rest, static friction on m_2 must supply

f_s=m_1g-m_2g\sin\theta

Rest is possible exactly when

\boxed{|m_1g-m_2g\sin\theta|\le \mu m_2g\cos\theta},

or, after canceling g,

\boxed{|m_1-m_2\sin\theta|\le \mu m_2\cos\theta}

If

m_1>m_2(\sin\theta+\mu\cos\theta),

then m_1 moves downward and m_2 moves up the incline. Friction on m_2 points down the incline:

\begin{cases} m_1g-T=m_1a,\\ T-m_2g\sin\theta-\mu m_2g\cos\theta=m_2a. \end{cases}

Adding the equations gives

\boxed{a=\frac{g\left[m_1-m_2(\sin\theta+\mu\cos\theta)\right]}{m_1+m_2}}

If

m_1<m_2(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta),

then m_1 moves upward and m_2 moves down the incline. With the same positive direction as before, the acceleration is negative:

\boxed{a=\frac{g\left[m_1-m_2\sin\theta+\mu m_2\cos\theta\right]}{m_1+m_2}<0}

The sign of a is part of the answer: it tells whether the initial direction assumption matches the actual motion.

Pendulum force components

A pendulum bob of mass m is attached to a massless string of length L. Let \theta be the angle from the downward vertical defined in Figure 7.

For the solution, put the pivot at the origin, with x to the right and y upward, and resolve the forces as in Figure 8.

The geometry gives

x=L\sin\theta, \qquad y=-L\cos\theta

The forces are tension T toward the pivot and gravity mg downward, so

F_x=-T\sin\theta, \qquad F_y=T\cos\theta-mg

Differentiate the coordinates twice:

\ddot x=L(\ddot\theta\cos\theta-\dot\theta^2\sin\theta), \qquad \ddot y=L(\ddot\theta\sin\theta+\dot\theta^2\cos\theta)

Newton’s second law gives

\begin{cases} mL(\ddot\theta\cos\theta-\dot\theta^2\sin\theta)=-T\sin\theta,\\ mL(\ddot\theta\sin\theta+\dot\theta^2\cos\theta)=T\cos\theta-mg. \end{cases}

Multiply the first equation by \cos\theta, multiply the second by \sin\theta, and add. The tension terms cancel:

mL\ddot\theta=-mg\sin\theta

Thus the angular equation of motion is

\boxed{\ddot\theta+\frac gL\sin\theta=0}

For small oscillations, \sin\theta\approx\theta, giving

\ddot\theta+\frac gL\theta=0, \qquad T_0=2\pi\sqrt{\frac Lg}

Frames

Use a coordinate transformation to distinguish a straight trajectory in an inertial frame from the curved trajectory seen in a rotating frame.

You and a friend stand at opposite ends of a diameter of a circular platform of radius R. The platform rotates counterclockwise at constant angular velocity \omega. At t=0, you throw a baseball toward your friend with speed v relative to you, as in Figure 9. Ignore gravity and air resistance. Find the trajectory seen by you.

Let (X,Y) be inertial coordinates centered on the platform. At t=0, put you at (-R,0) and your friend at (R,0). Your instantaneous velocity is (0,-\omega R), so the ball’s inertial initial velocity is

\vec V_0=(v,-\omega R)

The inertial initial velocity is obtained by the vector addition in Figure 10.

No real force acts on the ball, so its inertial trajectory is the straight line

X(t)=-R+vt, \qquad Y(t)=-\omega Rt

Let (x,y) be coordinates whose axes rotate with the platform but whose origin remains at its center. The axes have rotated through \theta=\omega t, so

\begin{pmatrix} x\\y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\omega t&\sin\omega t\\ -\sin\omega t&\cos\omega t \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} X\\Y \end{pmatrix}

Substituting the inertial trajectory gives

\begin{aligned} x(t)&=(-R+vt)\cos\omega t-\omega Rt\sin\omega t,\\ y(t)&=(R-vt)\sin\omega t-\omega Rt\cos\omega t. \end{aligned}

You remain fixed at (x,y)=(-R,0). Therefore, if (\xi,\eta) denotes the ball’s position relative to you, with \xi pointing from you toward the center at t=0, then

\boxed{ \begin{aligned} \xi(t)&=R+(-R+vt)\cos\omega t-\omega Rt\sin\omega t,\\ \eta(t)&=(R-vt)\sin\omega t-\omega Rt\cos\omega t. \end{aligned}}

This is the trajectory in your frame. It starts with

(\xi(0),\eta(0))=(0,0), \qquad (\dot\xi(0),\dot\eta(0))=(v,0),

so you initially see the ball moving directly toward your friend, who remains at (2R,0). The initial acceleration in your frame is

(\ddot\xi(0),\ddot\eta(0))=(-\omega^2R,-2\omega v)

The -2\omega v term is the Coriolis acceleration, which bends the apparent path sideways. The -\omega^2R term is the centrifugal acceleration at the ball’s initial position.

As a check, rotating (x,y) back through +\omega t recovers the inertial straight line (X,Y)=(-R+vt,-\omega Rt).

If instead the problem specifies that the ball moves along the fixed inertial X axis with velocity (u,0), then X=-R+ut and Y=0, and the trajectory seen from the platform is

x(t)=(-R+ut)\cos\omega t, \qquad y(t)=(R-ut)\sin\omega t

For the representative case u=\omega R, let \tau=\omega t. Then

\frac{x}{R}=(\tau-1)\cos\tau, \qquad \frac{y}{R}=(1-\tau)\sin\tau

During 0\le\tau\le2, the ball crosses the center at \tau=1 and reaches the rim again at \tau=2, tracing the curved path in Figure 11.

Energy and Momentum

Work

For a variable force, calculate work with an integral. For a conservative force such as a spring force, the work can also be written as the negative change in potential energy.

A 0.50\ \mathrm{kg} block is attached to a horizontal spring with spring constant k=200\ \mathrm{N/m}. The surface is frictionless. The block is held at x_i=0.10\ \mathrm m from equilibrium and released from rest. Find the work done by the spring and the speed of the block when it reaches x_f=0.060\ \mathrm m, with positions defined in Figure 12.

The spring force is

F_x=-kx

The signed area in Figure 13 represents the spring work from x_i to x_f.

Therefore, the work done by the spring is

\begin{aligned} W_s &=\int_{x_i}^{x_f}F_x\,dx \\ &=\int_{x_i}^{x_f}-kx\,dx \\ &=\frac12k\left(x_i^2-x_f^2\right) \\ &=\frac12(200)\left(0.10^2-0.060^2\right) \\ &=0.64\ \mathrm J. \end{aligned}

The work is positive because the spring force and the displacement both point toward equilibrium. By the work-energy theorem,

W_s=\Delta K =\frac12mv_f^2-\frac12mv_i^2

Since the block is released from rest, v_i=0, so

v_f =\sqrt{\frac{2W_s}{m}} =\sqrt{\frac{2(0.64)}{0.50}} =1.6\ \mathrm{m/s}

Define the spring potential energy by

U_s(x)=\frac12kx^2

Then

W_s =\frac12kx_i^2-\frac12kx_f^2 =-\Delta U_s

Combining W_s=\Delta K with W_s=-\Delta U_s gives

\Delta K+\Delta U_s=0,

or

\boxed{K+U_s =\frac12mv^2+\frac12kx^2 =E_{\text{mech}}=\text{constant}}

For this motion,

E_{\text{mech}} =\frac12k x_i^2 =1.0\ \mathrm J

At x_f=0.060\ \mathrm m,

K=0.64\ \mathrm J, \qquad U_s=\frac12(200)(0.060)^2=0.36\ \mathrm J,

and K+U_s=1.0\ \mathrm J, equal to the initial mechanical energy. This conservation law applies here because no nonconservative force, such as friction, does work on the block.

Kinetic Work-Energy Theorem

Use the work-energy theorem when forces and displacement are easier to relate than acceleration and time.

A 1200\ \mathrm{kg} car travels at 20\ \mathrm{m/s} on a level road. The brakes exert a constant 6000\ \mathrm N force opposite the motion. Neglect air resistance and rolling resistance. Find the stopping distance.

Choose the direction of motion as positive. Over a stopping distance d, the braking work is

W_{\text{brake}}=-F_bd

The normal force and gravity do no work because they are perpendicular to the horizontal displacement. Therefore,

\begin{aligned} W_{\text{net}} &=\Delta K \\ -F_bd &=K_f-K_i \\ &=0-\frac12mv_i^2. \end{aligned}

Solving for d gives

\begin{aligned} d &=\frac{mv_i^2}{2F_b} \\ &=\frac{(1200)(20)^2}{2(6000)} \\ &=40\ \mathrm m. \end{aligned}

Kinetic energy depends on speed rather than direction. The negative work removes the car’s initial kinetic energy.

Conservative Field

For a conservative force, first find a scalar potential satisfying \vec F=-\nabla U. Then work between two points depends only on the endpoints:

W_{A\to B}=-(U_B-U_A)

Potential from a 2-D force field

For coordinates measured in meters, let

\vec F(x,y)=2xy\,\hat i+(x^2-2y)\,\hat j

Determine whether the field is conservative, find its potential energy, and calculate the work done by the field from A=(0,0) to B=(2,1).

In a simply connected region, a two-dimensional field is conservative if

\frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y} =\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x}

Here,

\frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y}=2x, \qquad \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x}=2x,

so the field is conservative. From F_x=-\partial U/\partial x,

\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}=-2xy,

and integration with respect to x gives

U(x,y)=-x^2y+g(y)

Use F_y=-\partial U/\partial y:

x^2-2y =-\left(-x^2+g'(y)\right),

so g'(y)=2y and

U(x,y)=-x^2y+y^2+C

Therefore,

U_A=C, \qquad U_B=-2^2(1)+1^2+C=-3+C,

and the work is

W_{A\to B}=-(U_B-U_A)=3\ \mathrm J

The arbitrary constant cancels from every potential-energy difference.

Speed on a frictionless track

A small block is released from rest at height h_i=5.0\ \mathrm m and slides along the frictionless track in Figure 14 to height h_f=1.8\ \mathrm m. Find its speed at the lower point.

Gravity is conservative, while the normal force does no work. Thus mechanical energy is conserved:

K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f

Taking U_g=mgh and using v_i=0,

mgh_i=\frac12mv_f^2+mgh_f

The mass cancels, giving

\begin{aligned} v_f &=\sqrt{2g(h_i-h_f)} \\ &=\sqrt{2(9.8)(5.0-1.8)} \\ &\approx7.9\ \mathrm{m/s}. \end{aligned}

The result depends only on the change in height, not on the shape or length of the track. If friction were present, its work would have to be included separately as a change in mechanical energy.

Linear Momentum

For an isolated system, total momentum is conserved during every collision. Kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision.

Choose motion to the right as positive. A 2.0\ \mathrm{kg} cart moving at 3.0\ \mathrm{m/s} collides head-on with a stationary 1.0\ \mathrm{kg} cart.

Perfectly elastic collision

Let v_1 and v_2 be the carts’ velocities after the collision. Conservation of momentum gives

m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2,

so

2(3)+1(0)=2v_1+v_2

Because the collision is perfectly elastic, kinetic energy is also conserved. Equivalently, the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach:

v_2-v_1=u_1-u_2=3

Solving the two equations gives

v_1=1.0\ \mathrm{m/s}, \qquad v_2=4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}

Check the kinetic energy:

K_i =\frac12(2)(3^2) =9.0\ \mathrm J,

and

K_f =\frac12(2)(1^2)+\frac12(1)(4^2) =9.0\ \mathrm J

Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. The relative-speed equation is a convenient shortcut only for a one-dimensional perfectly elastic collision.

Perfectly inelastic collision

For a perfectly inelastic collision, the carts stick together and have a common final velocity v_f. Momentum conservation gives

m_1u_1+m_2u_2=(m_1+m_2)v_f

Therefore,

\begin{aligned} v_f &=\frac{m_1u_1+m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2} \\ &=\frac{(2)(3)+(1)(0)}{2+1} \\ &=2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}. \end{aligned}

The final kinetic energy is

K_f =\frac12(2+1)(2^2) =6.0\ \mathrm J

Thus

\Delta K=K_f-K_i=6.0-9.0=-3.0\ \mathrm J

Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not: 3.0\ \mathrm J is converted into deformation, heat, and sound. Sticking together identifies a perfectly inelastic collision; it does not mean that all kinetic energy is lost.

Impulse

Rocket equation

Use the impulse-momentum theorem over a short time interval to derive the one-dimensional rocket equation, including gravity but neglecting air resistance.

Consider a rocket moving vertically upward. At time t, its mass is m and its velocity is v. During the interval dt, it ejects a positive mass d\mu downward at speed u relative to the rocket. In this ideal model, u is also the effective exhaust velocity. The rocket’s mass and velocity then become

m-d\mu, \qquad v+dv

To apply the impulse-momentum theorem, take the system during this interval to be the rocket together with the mass it ejects. The exhaust has velocity v-u in the ground frame to first order. Thus

p_i=mv

and

p_f=(m-d\mu)(v+dv)+d\mu(v-u)

Neglecting the second-order product d\mu\,dv gives

p_f-p_i=m\,dv-u\,d\mu

Taking upward as positive, gravity supplies the external impulse

J_{\mathrm{ext}}=-mg\,dt

The impulse-momentum theorem therefore gives

m\,dv-u\,d\mu=-mg\,dt

Because the change in the rocket’s mass is dm=-d\mu,

m\,dv=-u\,dm-mg\,dt,

or

dv=-u\frac{dm}{m}-g\,dt

For constant effective exhaust velocity u and constant local gravitational acceleration g, integrate from (m_0,v_0,t_0) to (m_f,v_f,t_f):

\begin{aligned} v_f-v_0 &=-u\int_{m_0}^{m_f}\frac{dm}{m} -g\int_{t_0}^{t_f}dt \\ &=u\ln\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right) -g(t_f-t_0). \end{aligned}

Hence,

\boxed{v_f =v_0+u\ln\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)-g\Delta t} \qquad{(1)}

With no external force, the impulse term in Equation \href{#eq:rocket-equation-gravity}{\text{(1)}} vanishes. Define the ideal velocity increment as \Delta v_{\mathrm{ideal}}=v_f-v_0 in this no-external-force case. The ideal rocket equation is then

\boxed{\Delta v_{\mathrm{ideal}} =u\ln\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)} \qquad{(2)}

Define the positive propellant mass flow rate by

\dot m_p=\frac{d\mu}{dt}=-\frac{dm}{dt}>0

The ideal thrust is F=u\dot m_p. Rocket engines are commonly characterized by their specific impulse

I_{\mathrm{sp}} =\frac{F}{\dot m_p g_0},

where g_0=9.80665\ \mathrm{m/s^2} is standard gravity. Therefore,

\boxed{u =\frac{F}{\dot m_p} =g_0I_{\mathrm{sp}}} \qquad{(3)}

Here g_0 is a fixed conversion constant, not the local g in Equation \href{#eq:rocket-equation-gravity}{\text{(1)}}. For a real engine, u is the effective exhaust velocity: it may include pressure thrust and need not equal the exhaust gas velocity exactly.

The exhaust momentum must be included explicitly: applying \vec F=d(m\vec v)/dt directly to the variable-mass rocket alone omits the momentum carried away by the exhaust.

Single-stage mass limit

Use Equation \href{#eq:ideal-rocket-equation}{\text{(2)}} to explain why a chemically propelled single-stage-to-orbit rocket launched from Earth usually has an impractically small payload fraction.

Let the burnout mass consist of structural mass m_s and payload mass m_L:

m_f=m_s+m_L

Let \Delta v_{\mathrm{req}} be the ideal velocity increment that the propulsion system must supply. From Equation \href{#eq:ideal-rocket-equation}{\text{(2)}},

\frac{m_f}{m_0} =e^{-\Delta v_{\mathrm{req}}/u}

Define the structural fraction relative to the initial mass as

\sigma=\frac{m_s}{m_0}

The payload fraction is therefore

\boxed{ \frac{m_L}{m_0} =e^{-\Delta v_{\mathrm{req}}/u}-\sigma } \qquad{(4)}

For launch from Earth’s surface to low Earth orbit, a representative propulsion budget, including gravity and aerodynamic losses, is

\Delta v_{\mathrm{req}}=9.4\ \mathrm{km/s}

This value is inserted as \Delta v_{\mathrm{req}} in the ideal rocket equation, so the losses must not be subtracted a second time using Equation \href{#eq:rocket-equation-gravity}{\text{(1)}}.

For a high-performance chemical engine with I_{\mathrm{sp}}=450\ \mathrm s, Equation \href{#eq:specific-impulse-exhaust-speed}{\text{(3)}} gives

u=g_0I_{\mathrm{sp}} =(9.81)(450) \approx4.41\ \mathrm{km/s}

The required mass ratio and burnout fraction follow from Equation \href{#eq:ideal-rocket-equation}{\text{(2)}}:

\frac{m_0}{m_f} =e^{\Delta v_{\mathrm{req}}/u} =e^{9.4/4.41} \approx8.4, \qquad \frac{m_f}{m_0} \approx0.119

Only 11.9\% of the initial mass remains for the structure and payload. If \sigma=0.10, Equation \href{#eq:single-stage-payload-fraction}{\text{(4)}} gives

\frac{m_L}{m_0} \approx0.119-0.100 =0.019

The payload is only about 1.9\% of the launch mass. With a lower specific impulse of 350\ \mathrm s,

u\approx3.43\ \mathrm{km/s}, \qquad \frac{m_f}{m_0} =e^{-9.4/3.43} \approx0.064

In that case, a structural fraction greater than 6.4\% leaves no mass for payload at all.

Staging does not change the rocket equation. It improves the payload fraction by discarding empty tanks and engines, so later stages do not expend propellant accelerating those inactive structures. The calculation does not prove that every single-stage rocket is undesirable; it shows why chemical single-stage launch from Earth to orbit is usually unattractive under realistic structural constraints.

Rotation

Position, Velocity, Acceleration

A flywheel initially rotates at

\omega_0=20\ \mathrm{rad/s}

It brakes with constant angular acceleration

\alpha=-2.5\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}

Find the stopping time and the angular displacement before it stops.

Since \alpha=\mathrm d\omega/\mathrm dt is constant,

\omega(t)=\omega_0+\alpha t

At the stopping time t_s, \omega(t_s)=0, so

\boxed{ t_s=-\frac{\omega_0}{\alpha} =-\frac{20}{-2.5} =8.0\ \mathrm s }

The angular displacement follows from \omega=\mathrm d\theta/\mathrm dt:

\begin{aligned} \Delta\theta &=\int_0^{t_s}\omega(t)\,dt \\ &=\int_0^8(20-2.5t)\,dt \\ &=\left[20t-1.25t^2\right]_0^8 \\ &=80\ \mathrm{rad}. \end{aligned}

Thus

\boxed{ N=\frac{\Delta\theta}{2\pi} =\frac{80}{2\pi} \approx12.7\ \text{revolutions} }

The negative sign of \alpha indicates that the angular velocity decreases; it does not make the accumulated angular displacement negative.

Moment of Inertia

For a continuous body rotating about a specified axis, divide the body into mass elements and integrate the squared perpendicular distance to that axis:

I=\int r_\perp^2\,dm

The axis must always be stated because the same body has different moments of inertia about different axes.

Direct integration

Choose a mass density suited to the body’s geometry, express dm in the corresponding coordinates, and integrate r_\perp^2\,dm.

slender rod

Derive the moment of inertia of a uniform slender rod of length L and mass M about an axis through its center and perpendicular to the rod.

Place the rod on the x-axis with its center at the origin. Its linear mass density is

\lambda=\frac{M}{L}, \qquad dm=\lambda\,dx

Every mass element is a perpendicular distance |x| from the axis, so

\begin{aligned} I_{\mathrm{cm}} &=\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}x^2\lambda\,dx \\ &=\frac{M}{L}\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-L/2}^{L/2} \\ &=\boxed{\frac{1}{12}ML^2}. \end{aligned}

For comparison, if the perpendicular axis passes through one end, choose that end as x=0:

I_{\mathrm{end}} =\frac{M}{L}\int_0^L x^2\,dx =\boxed{\frac13ML^2}

rectangular lamina

Derive the moment of inertia of a uniform thin rectangular lamina of side lengths a and b about an axis through its center and perpendicular to its plane.

Place the lamina in the xy-plane, with the sides parallel to the coordinate axes. Its surface mass density is

\sigma=\frac{M}{ab}, \qquad dm=\sigma\,dx\,dy

Because r_\perp^2=x^2+y^2,

\begin{aligned} I_z &=\sigma \int_{-a/2}^{a/2}\int_{-b/2}^{b/2} (x^2+y^2)\,dy\,dx \\ &=\sigma\left( b\int_{-a/2}^{a/2}x^2\,dx +a\int_{-b/2}^{b/2}y^2\,dy \right) \\ &=\frac{M}{ab}\left( \frac{ba^3}{12}+\frac{ab^3}{12} \right) \\ &=\boxed{\frac{1}{12}M(a^2+b^2)}. \end{aligned}

thin spherical shell

Derive the moment of inertia of a uniform thin spherical shell of radius R and mass M about a diameter.

Take the rotation axis to be the z-axis. A surface element at polar angle \theta has perpendicular distance R\sin\theta from the axis. With uniform surface density,

\sigma=\frac{M}{4\pi R^2}, \qquad dm=\sigma R^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi

Therefore,

\begin{aligned} I_z &=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi (R\sin\theta)^2 \sigma R^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi \\ &=2\pi\sigma R^4 \int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\,d\theta \\ &=2\pi\sigma R^4\left(\frac43\right) \\ &=\boxed{\frac23MR^2}. \end{aligned}

The distance in the integral is the distance to the chosen diameter, not the constant distance R to the center.

solid sphere

Derive the moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere of radius R and mass M about a diameter by treating it as a stack of thin spherical shells.

The volume mass density is

\rho=\frac{M}{\frac43\pi R^3} =\frac{3M}{4\pi R^3}

A shell of radius r and thickness dr has mass

dm=4\pi r^2\rho\,dr

Using the thin-shell result for each shell,

\begin{aligned} I &=\int_0^R \frac23r^2\,dm \\ &=\frac23\int_0^R r^2(4\pi r^2\rho\,dr) \\ &=\frac{8\pi\rho}{3}\int_0^Rr^4\,dr \\ &=\frac{8\pi\rho R^5}{15} \\ &=\boxed{\frac25MR^2}. \end{aligned}

Although both objects have the same outer radius, the solid sphere has the smaller coefficient because more of its mass lies close to the axis.

The axis theorems replace a new volume or surface integral with moments of inertia about axes that are easier to evaluate.

Parallel-axis theorem

Let an axis through the center of mass be parallel to a second axis a perpendicular distance d away. For a mass element, let \boldsymbol{\rho}_\perp be its position relative to the center of mass, projected onto the plane perpendicular to the axes, and let \mathbf d point from the center-of-mass axis to the displaced axis. Figure 15 fixes the directions of these vectors in that perpendicular plane.

The position of the mass element relative to the displaced axis is

\mathbf r_\perp=\boldsymbol{\rho}_\perp-\mathbf d

The moment of inertia about the displaced axis is

\begin{aligned} I &=\int |\boldsymbol{\rho}_\perp-\mathbf d|^2\,dm \\ &=\int \rho_\perp^2\,dm -2\mathbf d\mathbin{\cdot}\int\boldsymbol{\rho}_\perp\,dm +d^2\int dm. \end{aligned}

The origin of \boldsymbol{\rho} is the center of mass, so

\int\boldsymbol{\rho}\,dm=\mathbf 0,

and its perpendicular projection also integrates to zero. Since \int dm=M,

\boxed{I=I_{\mathrm{cm}}+Md^2}

For the slender rod, shifting the axis from its center to one end gives d=L/2 and

I_{\mathrm{end}} =\frac{1}{12}ML^2+M\left(\frac L2\right)^2 =\frac13ML^2,

in agreement with the direct integral. The reference axis must pass through the center of mass; the formula does not apply between two arbitrary parallel axes.

Perpendicular-axis theorem

Consider a thin lamina confined to the xy-plane. Let the x- and y-axes lie in the lamina and let the z-axis pass through their intersection perpendicular to the lamina, as defined in Figure 16.

For a mass element at (x,y),

r_z^2=x^2+y^2, \qquad r_x^2=y^2, \qquad r_y^2=x^2

Therefore,

\begin{aligned} I_z &=\int(x^2+y^2)\,dm \\ &=\int y^2\,dm+\int x^2\,dm \\ &=\boxed{I_x+I_y}. \end{aligned}

For the rectangular lamina,

I_x=\frac{1}{12}Mb^2, \qquad I_y=\frac{1}{12}Ma^2,

so

I_z=I_x+I_y =\frac{1}{12}M(a^2+b^2),

matching the direct double integral. This theorem requires a planar body; for a three-dimensional body, a mass element generally has a nonzero coordinate perpendicular to the chosen plane, so the relation does not hold.

Torque

A uniform slender rod of length L and mass M extends horizontally to the right from a fixed pivot at its left end. It is released from rest under gravity. Find the initial acceleration of the rod’s right endpoint. Figure 17 defines the initial geometry.

The rod’s weight Mg acts at its center of mass, a distance L/2 from the pivot. Gravity therefore turns the rod clockwise, not counterclockwise. Taking clockwise as positive, the initial torque is

\displaystyle \tau_0=Mg\frac L2

The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about one end is

I_{\mathrm{end}}=\frac13ML^2

Therefore, the initial angular acceleration is

\alpha_0 =\frac{\tau_0}{I_{\mathrm{end}}} =\frac{MgL/2}{ML^2/3} =\frac{3g}{2L}

Because the rod starts from rest, \omega_0=0, so the endpoint initially has no radial acceleration. Its acceleration is purely tangential:

\boxed{\vec a_{\mathrm{right},0}=-\frac32g\,\hat y},

where \hat y points upward. Thus, the endpoint’s initial acceleration has magnitude 3g/2 and points downward. The result is independent of L and M: increasing L increases both the gravitational torque and the rotational inertia in the combination that cancels from the endpoint acceleration.

Work–Energy Theorem

For rotation about a fixed axis, net torque does work through angular displacement:

W_{\text{net}} =\int_{\theta_i}^{\theta_f}\tau_{\text{net}}\,d\theta =\Delta K_{\text{rot}}

A uniform solid sphere of mass m and radius R is released from rest at vertical height h and rolls without slipping down an incline. Assume static friction is sufficient to maintain pure rolling, and neglect rolling resistance and other energy losses. Find the sphere’s speed at the bottom.

Static friction supplies the torque needed for rolling but does no work in ideal pure rolling, so mechanical energy is conserved:

mgh =\frac12mv^2+\frac12I\omega^2

For a uniform solid sphere,

I=\frac25mR^2, \qquad v=R\omega

Therefore,

\begin{aligned} mgh &=\frac12mv^2 +\frac12\left(\frac25mR^2\right)\left(\frac vR\right)^2 \\ &=\frac7{10}mv^2, \end{aligned}

and the speed at the bottom is

\boxed{v=\sqrt{\frac{10gh}{7}}}

The mass and radius cancel. The radius affects the moment of inertia and angular speed in compensating ways.

Angular Momentum

For a rigid body rotating about a fixed principal axis, use L=I\omega; if the net external torque is zero, angular momentum is conserved.

Figure skater

A spinning skater has moment of inertia I_i=4.0\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} and angular velocity \omega_i=2.0\ \mathrm{rad/s}. The skater pulls in their arms, reducing the moment of inertia to I_f=1.6\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}. Find the final angular velocity if the external torque about the spin axis is negligible.

Angular momentum is conserved:

I_i\omega_i=I_f\omega_f

Therefore,

\boxed{ \omega_f =\frac{I_i\omega_i}{I_f} =\frac{(4.0)(2.0)}{1.6} =5.0\ \mathrm{rad/s} }

Reducing the moment of inertia increases the angular velocity while leaving L unchanged.

Procession

A rapidly spinning symmetric top has mass M, moment of inertia I about its spin axis, and spin angular velocity \omega_{spin}. Its center of mass is a horizontal distance h from the support point. Derive the steady procession angular velocity.

Figure 18 uses an oblique projection to show the symmetric top and the cone swept out by its angular momentum. Straight arrows specify the positive rotation axes, while small curved arrows show the corresponding senses of rotation.

The magnitude of the gravitational torque about the support is

{\tau}_O=Mgh

For rapid spin about a principal axis, the top’s spin angular momentum has magnitude

L_{spin}=I\omega_{spin}

During a short time dt, steady procession turns \vec L_{spin} through the small angle d\phi without changing its magnitude. This is because \vec\tau_O is perpendicular to the \vec\omega_{spin} axis and hence to \vec L_{spin}, so d\vec L=\vec\tau_O\,dt changes only the direction of \vec L_{spin}. Therefore,

|d\vec L|=L_{spin}\,d\phi

Using \vec\tau_O=d\vec L/dt,

\begin{aligned} {\tau}_O &=\frac{|d\vec L|}{dt} \\ &=L_{spin}\frac{d\phi}{dt} \\ &=L_{spin}\omega_{procession}. \end{aligned}

Substitute \tau_O=Mgh and L_{spin}=I\omega_{spin}:

\boxed{ \omega_{procession} =\frac{\tau_O}{L_{spin}} =\frac{Mgh}{I\omega_{spin}} }

The approximation requires

\boxed{\omega_{spin}\gg\omega_{procession}},

so the top completes many spin rotations during one slow procession cycle. Because \vec\tau_O\perp\vec L_{spin}, gravity changes the direction of the spin angular momentum rather than its magnitude in this steady approximation.

Equilibrium and Elasticity

Static Equilibrium

Beam supported by a cable

In two dimensions, static equilibrium gives three scalar equations:

\sum F_x=0, \qquad \sum F_y=0, \qquad \sum\tau_O=0

In a uniform gravitational field, treat the weight M\vec g as acting at the center of mass. When the net force is zero, the net torque is independent of the choice of origin, so choose the torque origin to simplify the calculation.

A uniform horizontal beam of length L and mass M is attached to a wall by an ideal hinge at O. A cable attached to the other end makes an angle \theta above the beam. A load of mass m hangs from the beam at distance a from the hinge, as shown in Figure 19. Find the cable tension T and the horizontal and vertical hinge forces R_x and R_y.

Isolate the beam. Figure 20 shows the external forces: the hinge reactions, the cable tension, the beam’s weight at its center of mass, and the force from the load.

Take counterclockwise torque as positive. Choosing the hinge as the torque origin removes both unknown hinge forces from the torque equation:

\sum\tau_O =TL\sin\theta-Mg\frac L2-mga =0

Therefore,

\boxed{ T=\frac{MgL/2+mga}{L\sin\theta} }

Force balance in the horizontal and vertical directions gives

\begin{aligned} \sum F_x&=R_x-T\cos\theta=0 \\ \sum F_y&=R_y+T\sin\theta-(M+m)g=0 \end{aligned}

Hence,

\boxed{ R_x=T\cos\theta, \qquad R_y=\frac{Mg}{2}+mg\left(1-\frac aL\right) }

The cable tension grows without bound as \theta\to0: a nearly horizontal cable supplies very little upward force. The hinge is the useful torque origin because its two unknown reaction forces have zero moment arm about that point.

Inverted-pendulum stability

A rider and self-balancing scooter are modeled as one rigid inverted pendulum pivoting about the tire contact point. Their total mass is M=80.0\ \mathrm{kg}, the center of mass is h=0.850\ \mathrm m above the pivot, and the moment of inertia about the pivot is I=55.0\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}. Let \vartheta=0 be the upright position. After a power failure, the scooter is released from rest at \vartheta_0=1.00^\circ. Ignore wheel translation and find the stability of the upright equilibrium and the time to reach 5.00^\circ and 10.0^\circ.

Figure 21 defines the inverted-pendulum geometry without assuming the direction of the angular acceleration.

The gravitational potential energy is

U(\vartheta)=Mgh\cos\vartheta

At the upright position,

U'(0)=0, \qquad U''(0)=-Mgh<0

Thus the upright state is an unstable equilibrium. Gravity drives a small positive lean farther from vertical:

Figure 22 shows the gravitational force and its moment arm about the contact point.

I\ddot\vartheta=Mgh\sin\vartheta\simeq Mgh\vartheta

Write the linearized equation as

\ddot\vartheta=\frac{\vartheta}{t_{\mathrm{inst}}^2}, \qquad t_{\mathrm{inst}}=\sqrt{\frac{I}{Mgh}}

For the stated parameters,

t_{\mathrm{inst}}=\sqrt{\frac{I}{Mgh}} =\sqrt{\frac{55.0}{(80.0)(9.81)(0.850)}} =0.287\ \mathrm s

The general linearized motion is a sum of growing and decaying modes:

\vartheta(t)=C_+e^{t/t_{\mathrm{inst}}} +C_-e^{-t/t_{\mathrm{inst}}}

Thus t_{\mathrm{inst}} is the inverse exponential growth rate: during each interval t_{\mathrm{inst}}, the growing mode is multiplied by e. It is not the time at which the scooter falls; that time also depends on the initial disturbance and the chosen failure angle. With \dot\vartheta(0)=0, the two modes combine to give

\vartheta(t)=\vartheta_0\cosh\frac{t}{t_{\mathrm{inst}}}

Hence the time to reach an angle \vartheta_f is

t=t_{\mathrm{inst}}\operatorname{arcosh}\frac{\vartheta_f}{\vartheta_0}

For the two thresholds,

\begin{aligned} t_{5^\circ} &=(0.287)\operatorname{arcosh}(5)=0.658\ \mathrm s, \\ t_{10^\circ} &=(0.287)\operatorname{arcosh}(10)=0.859\ \mathrm s \end{aligned}

The controller must react on a time scale short compared with t_{\mathrm{inst}}. A larger moment of inertia slows the departure from upright, while a larger gravitational lever Mgh accelerates it.

Stress and Strain

A rectangular element with side strains \epsilon_x, \epsilon_y, and \epsilon_z changes volume from V to

V'=V(1+\epsilon_x)(1+\epsilon_y)(1+\epsilon_z)

For small strains, products of strains are negligible, so

\boxed{ \epsilon_V =\frac{V'-V}{V} \simeq\epsilon_x+\epsilon_y+\epsilon_z }

Elastic Moduli

Linearity allows stresses to be superposed. Isotropy means that the same Young’s modulus E and Poisson’s ratio \nu apply along every direction.

Isotropic Hooke’s law

Pull a rod along the x direction while its side surfaces remain free:

\sigma_x>0, \qquad \sigma_y=\sigma_z=0

Young’s modulus gives the strain along the applied stress:

\epsilon_x=\frac{\sigma_x}{E}

Poisson’s ratio gives the strain perpendicular to the applied stress. Because an isotropic material responds equally in the y and z directions,

\epsilon_y=\epsilon_z =-\nu\epsilon_x =-\nu\frac{\sigma_x}{E}

Thus a positive tensile stress lengthens the rod in x and narrows it in y and z.

Write the corresponding result for loads along y and z, then add the three responses. For simultaneous normal stresses,

\boxed{ \begin{aligned} \epsilon_x &=\frac{1}{E}\left[\sigma_x-\nu(\sigma_y+\sigma_z)\right], \\ \epsilon_y &=\frac{1}{E}\left[\sigma_y-\nu(\sigma_z+\sigma_x)\right], \\ \epsilon_z &=\frac{1}{E}\left[\sigma_z-\nu(\sigma_x+\sigma_y)\right] \end{aligned} } \qquad{(5)}

This equation is the common starting point for the bulk- and shear-modulus relations.

Bulk modulus

An increase in hydrostatic pressure applies the same compressive stress in all three directions:

\sigma_x=\sigma_y=\sigma_z=-\Delta p

Substitute these stresses into Equation 5:

\begin{aligned} \epsilon_x &=\frac{1}{E}\left[-\Delta p-\nu(-\Delta p-\Delta p)\right] \\ &=-\frac{(1-2\nu)\Delta p}{E} \end{aligned}

By symmetry, \epsilon_y=\epsilon_z=\epsilon_x. For small strains, \epsilon_V\simeq\epsilon_x+\epsilon_y+\epsilon_z, so

\epsilon_V =-\frac{3(1-2\nu)\Delta p}{E}

Using B=-\Delta p/\epsilon_V gives

\boxed{B=\frac{E}{3(1-2\nu)}} \qquad{(6)}

Shear modulus

Use a plane-stress model: the square represents a small element of a thin plate loaded only in the xy plane. Its surfaces normal to z are free, so

\sigma_{zz}=\tau_{xz}=\tau_{yz}=0

The square is therefore an xy view of a three-dimensional material element, not a two-dimensional material.

The in-plane stress components form the matrix

\boldsymbol\sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_{xx}&\tau_{xy}\\ \tau_{yx}&\sigma_{yy} \end{pmatrix}

The first subscript gives the direction of the traction component, and the second gives the direction of the face normal. Thus the diagonal entries \sigma_{xx} and \sigma_{yy} are normal stresses, while the off-diagonal entries \tau_{xy} and \tau_{yx} are shear stresses. Figure 23 shows the four components; arrows on the opposite faces are equal and opposite.

For a cut whose unit normal is

\hat n=n_x\hat x+n_y\hat y,

the force per unit area acting across the cut is the traction vector

\boxed{ \mathbf t(\hat n) =\boldsymbol\sigma\hat n = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_{xx}n_x+\sigma_{xy}n_y\\ \sigma_{yx}n_x+\sigma_{yy}n_y \end{pmatrix} }

For an ordinary continuum without couple stresses, angular-momentum balance requires \boldsymbol\sigma=\boldsymbol\sigma^{\mathsf T}, so \sigma_{xy}=\sigma_{yx}.

Figure 24 shows the forces in pure shear and the resulting extension and contraction along the diagonal directions.

Pure shear is the special case \sigma_{xx}=\sigma_{yy}=0 and \tau_{xy}=\tau_{yx}=\tau, so the stress matrix for panel (a) is

\boldsymbol\sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 0&\tau\\ \tau&0 \end{pmatrix}

Choose unit vectors along the diagonals in panel (b):

\hat e_1=\frac{\hat x+\hat y}{\sqrt2}, \qquad \hat e_2=\frac{-\hat x+\hat y}{\sqrt2}

The normal and shear stresses in these directions are

\begin{aligned} \sigma_1&=\hat e_1\mathbin{\cdot}\boldsymbol\sigma\hat e_1=+\tau,\\ \sigma_2&=\hat e_2\mathbin{\cdot}\boldsymbol\sigma\hat e_2=-\tau,\\ \tau_{12}&=\hat e_1\mathbin{\cdot}\boldsymbol\sigma\hat e_2=0 \end{aligned}

Thus direction 1 is under tension, direction 2 is under compression, and there is no shear stress on the rotated faces. Apply Equation 5 along directions 1 and 2:

\begin{aligned} \epsilon_1 &=\frac{1}{E}\left[\tau-\nu(-\tau+0)\right] =\frac{(1+\nu)\tau}{E}, \\ \epsilon_2 &=\frac{1}{E}\left[-\tau-\nu(\tau+0)\right] =-\frac{(1+\nu)\tau}{E} \end{aligned}

Panel (b) shows the same result geometrically. For small deformation, the engineering shear strain is the diagonal extension minus the diagonal contraction:

\gamma=\epsilon_1-\epsilon_2 =\frac{2(1+\nu)\tau}{E}

Using G=\tau/\gamma gives

\boxed{G=\frac{E}{2(1+\nu)}} \qquad{(7)}

Relations among moduli

Equations 6 and 7 give

E=3B(1-2\nu), \qquad E=2G(1+\nu)

Eliminate \nu:

\nu =\frac{E}{2G}-1 =\frac12-\frac{E}{6B}

Therefore,

\boxed{E=\frac{9BG}{3B+G}}

Thus any two of E, G, B, and \nu determine the other two. This result requires isotropic, linear elastic behavior. A fluid at rest has G=0 but may have B>0.

Elastic Energy

A thin iron rod of length L and cross-sectional area A is fixed at one end. A tensile force F extends it by \Delta L. Assume the rod remains in its linear elastic range.

Young’s modulus gives

E =\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon} =\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}

Therefore,

F=\frac{EA}{L}\Delta L

This has the spring form F=kx, with

\boxed{k_{\mathrm{rod}}=\frac{EA}{L}}

The stored elastic energy is

\boxed{ U =\frac12F\Delta L =\frac12\frac{EA}{L}(\Delta L)^2 }

Since the rod volume is AL, its energy density is

u=\frac{U}{AL} =\frac12E\left(\frac{\Delta L}{L}\right)^2 =\frac12E\epsilon^2

For a numerical example, take

d=1.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m, \qquad L=1.00\ \mathrm m, \qquad F=100\ \mathrm N, \qquad E=200\ \mathrm{GPa}

The cross-sectional area and equivalent spring constant are

\begin{aligned} A&=\frac{\pi d^2}{4} =7.85\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^2}, \\ k_{\mathrm{rod}}&=\frac{EA}{L} =1.57\times10^5\ \mathrm{N/m} \end{aligned}

The stress, extension, and stored energy are

\begin{aligned} \sigma&=\frac FA =1.27\times10^8\ \mathrm{Pa}, \\ \Delta L&=\frac{F}{k_{\mathrm{rod}}} =6.37\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm m, \\ U&=\frac12F\Delta L =3.18\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm J \end{aligned}

If the yield stress is 250\ \mathrm{MPa}, the corresponding force is

F_y=\sigma_yA =(250\times10^6)(7.85\times10^{-7}) \approx196\ \mathrm N

Since 100\ \mathrm N<196\ \mathrm N, the rod remains in the elastic range under this material assumption.

Gravitation

Universal Gravitation

Treat gravitation as a vector interaction. For several point masses, first determine the direction from the test mass toward each source mass, then add the individual force vectors.

Weighing Earth

At two locations approximately on the same meridian, the difference between the Sun’s noon zenith angles is 7.2^\circ, and the surface distance between the locations is 800\ \mathrm{km}. Use these measurements together with

g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}, \qquad G=6.67430\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}

to estimate Earth’s mean radius R_E and mass M_E.

Because sunlight arriving at Earth is nearly parallel, the zenith-angle difference is also the central angle subtended by the surface arc. Convert it to radians:

\theta =7.2^\circ\left(\frac{\pi\ \mathrm{rad}}{180^\circ}\right) \approx0.1257\ \mathrm{rad}

For an arc of length s=R_E\theta,

R_E =\frac{s}{\theta} =\frac{8.00\times10^5\ \mathrm m}{0.1257} \approx6.37\times10^6\ \mathrm m

At Earth’s surface, Newton’s law of gravitation and the measured weight of a test mass describe the same force:

G\frac{M_E m}{R_E^2}=mg

The test mass cancels, giving

\begin{aligned} M_E &=\frac{gR_E^2}{G} \\ &=\frac{(9.81)(6.37\times10^6)^2} {6.67430\times10^{-11}} \\ &\approx\boxed{5.96\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg}}. \end{aligned}

The angle must be expressed in radians in s=R_E\theta. Measurements of g and R_E determine GM_E; determining M_E separately also requires a laboratory measurement of G.

Earth–Moon balance point

Earth and the Moon have masses

M_E=5.97\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg}, \qquad M_M=7.35\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{kg},

and their center-to-center separation is D=3.84\times10^8\ \mathrm m. Ignoring their orbital motion, find the point between them where a small test mass experiences zero net gravitational force.

Let x be the distance from Earth’s center to the test mass. Its distance from the Moon is D-x. Between the two bodies, the forces point in opposite directions, so they cancel when their magnitudes are equal:

G\frac{M_E m}{x^2} =G\frac{M_M m}{(D-x)^2}

Cancel Gm and take the positive square root:

\frac{\sqrt{M_E}}{x} =\frac{\sqrt{M_M}}{D-x}

Solving for x gives

\begin{aligned} D-x &=x\sqrt{\frac{M_M}{M_E}}, \\ x &=\frac{D}{1+\sqrt{M_M/M_E}} \\ &\approx\boxed{3.46\times10^8\ \mathrm m}. \end{aligned}

Thus the point is approximately

D-x\approx\boxed{3.84\times10^7\ \mathrm m}

from the Moon’s center. The test mass cancels, as required by the equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass. This static balance point is not the Earth–Moon L_1 point: locating L_1 requires the centripetal acceleration of a body co-rotating with Earth and the Moon.

Gravitational Field

A uniform thin spherical shell has radius R and mass M. For a point P at distance r from the center, derive \Phi(r) and \mathbf g(r) inside and outside the shell, with \Phi(\infty)=0.

Figure 25 shows the ring element used to sum the potential.

Choose OP as the polar axis. With surface density \sigma=M/(4\pi R^2), a ring at polar angle \theta has mass \mathrm dm and distance s from P given by

\mathrm dm =2\pi\sigma R^2\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta, \qquad s(\theta) =\sqrt{R^2+r^2-2Rr\cos\theta}

Potential is a scalar, so the ring contributions add directly:

\begin{aligned} \Phi(r) &=-G\int\frac{\mathrm dm}{s} \\ &=-2\pi G\sigma R^2 \int_0^\pi \frac{\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta} {\sqrt{R^2+r^2-2Rr\cos\theta}}. \end{aligned}

For s^2=R^2+r^2-2Rr\cos\theta,

s\,\mathrm ds=Rr\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta, \qquad s(0)=|R-r|, \qquad s(\pi)=R+r

Thus, for r>0,

\begin{aligned} \Phi(r) &=-\frac{2\pi G\sigma R}{r} \int_{|R-r|}^{R+r}\mathrm ds \\ &=-\frac{2\pi G\sigma R}{r} \left[(R+r)-|R-r|\right]. \end{aligned}

Using M=4\pi R^2\sigma gives

\boxed{ \Phi(r)= \begin{cases} -\dfrac{GM}{R},&0\le r\le R,\\[6pt] -\dfrac{GM}{r},&r\ge R. \end{cases} } \qquad{(8)}

The r=0 value follows by continuity, and the two branches agree at r=R. Spherical symmetry gives

\mathbf g(r) =-\frac{\mathrm d\Phi}{\mathrm dr}\hat r,

and therefore

\boxed{ \mathbf g(r)= \begin{cases} \mathbf 0,&0\le r<R,\\[4pt] -\dfrac{GM}{r^2}\hat r,&r>R. \end{cases} } \qquad{(9)}

Figure 26 plots both results, with g_r=\mathbf g\cdot\hat r.

The potential is continuous at r=R, whereas the field has a jump because the mass lies on an ideal surface. Inside, \mathbf g=\mathbf 0 but \Phi=-GM/R: zero field means constant potential, not zero potential. Moving a test mass between interior points changes no potential energy; moving it quasistatically to infinity requires work GMm/R.

Kepler’s Laws

The following four exercises give a step-by-step derivation of Kepler’s laws.

Consider two isolated point masses M and m at positions \mathbf r_M and \mathbf r_m. Assume a collision-free orbit with nonzero angular momentum.

Relative motion and equal areas

Reduce the two-body problem to one equation for the relative position, then prove Kepler’s second law.

Relative equation of motion

Define the relative position, velocity, and separation:

\mathbf r=\mathbf r_m-\mathbf r_M, \qquad \mathbf v=\dot{\mathbf r}, \qquad r=|\mathbf r|

Figure 27 shows the direction convention for the three position vectors.

The vector \mathbf r points from M to m. Newton’s second law for each body gives

\ddot{\mathbf r}_M =\frac{Gm}{r^3}\mathbf r, \qquad \ddot{\mathbf r}_m =-\frac{GM}{r^3}\mathbf r

Subtracting the two accelerations gives

\begin{aligned} \ddot{\mathbf r} &=\ddot{\mathbf r}_m-\ddot{\mathbf r}_M \\ &=-\frac{G(M+m)}{r^3}\mathbf r. \end{aligned}

Define the gravitational parameter \mu_g=G(M+m). The relative equation of motion is

\boxed{ \ddot{\mathbf r} =-\frac{\mu_g}{r^3}\mathbf r } \qquad{(10)}

Planar motion and angular momentum

Define the specific angular momentum of the relative motion:

\mathbf h=\mathbf r\times\mathbf v

Equation \href{#eq:kepler-relative-motion}{\text{(10)}} is a central-force equation: \ddot{\mathbf r} is parallel to \mathbf r. Therefore,

\begin{aligned} \dot{\mathbf h} &=\mathbf v\times\mathbf v +\mathbf r\times\ddot{\mathbf r} \\ &=\mathbf 0. \end{aligned}

The definition of \mathbf h also gives

\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf h =\mathbf r\cdot(\mathbf r\times\mathbf v) =0

Hence every \mathbf r(t) lies in the plane through the origin perpendicular to \mathbf h. Because \mathbf h is constant and nonzero, this plane is fixed; the relative motion is planar.

Equal-area law

Figure 28 shows the differential area element and the corresponding finite equal-area statement.

During \mathrm dt, the relative displacement is \mathrm d\mathbf r=\mathbf v\,\mathrm dt. The line joining the bodies therefore sweeps out

\mathrm dA =\frac12|\mathbf r\times\mathbf v|\,\mathrm dt

The areal velocity is

\boxed{ \frac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dt} =\frac12|\mathbf r\times\mathbf v| =\frac h2 =\text{constant} }, \qquad{(11)}

where h=|\mathbf h|. A constant areal velocity implies equal swept areas in equal time intervals: Kepler’s second law. This result requires only a central force, not the inverse-square form.

Orbit equation and conic sections

Use the inverse-square term in Equation \href{#eq:kepler-relative-motion}{\text{(10)}} to derive the relative orbit.

Polar kinematics

Choose polar coordinates (r,\theta) in the orbital plane, with \theta increasing along the motion. Figure 29 defines the moving polar basis.

The Cartesian unit vectors \hat i and \hat j are fixed, but the polar unit vectors rotate with \theta:

\hat r=\cos\theta\,\hat i+\sin\theta\,\hat j, \qquad \hat\theta=-\sin\theta\,\hat i+\cos\theta\,\hat j

Differentiate with respect to \theta:

\frac{\mathrm d\hat r}{\mathrm d\theta} =-\sin\theta\,\hat i+\cos\theta\,\hat j =\hat\theta, \qquad \frac{\mathrm d\hat\theta}{\mathrm d\theta} =-\cos\theta\,\hat i-\sin\theta\,\hat j =-\hat r

The chain rule gives the corresponding time derivatives:

\dot{\hat r}=\dot\theta\,\hat\theta, \qquad \dot{\hat\theta}=-\dot\theta\,\hat r

Differentiating \mathbf r=r\hat r gives the velocity

\dot{\mathbf r} =\dot r\,\hat r+r\dot\theta\,\hat\theta,

and acceleration

\ddot{\mathbf r} =\left(\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2\right)\hat r +\left(r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta\right)\hat\theta

Polar equations of motion

Substitute \mathbf r=r\hat r into Equation \href{#eq:kepler-relative-motion}{\text{(10)}}:

\left(\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2\right)\hat r +\left(r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta\right)\hat\theta =-\frac{\mu_g}{r^2}\hat r

Because the right-hand side has no \hat\theta component, equating the coefficients of the orthogonal basis vectors gives the radial equation

\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2 =-\frac{\mu_g}{r^2} \qquad{(12)}

and the tangential equation

r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta=0

Multiplying the tangential equation by r gives

\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(r^2\dot\theta\right) =r^2\ddot\theta+2r\dot r\dot\theta =0

This constant is the magnitude of the specific angular momentum. Substitute the polar forms of \mathbf r and \dot{\mathbf r} and use the bilinearity of the cross product:

\begin{aligned} \mathbf h &=\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r} \\ &=(r\hat r)\times \left(\dot r\,\hat r+r\dot\theta\,\hat\theta\right) \\ &=(r\hat r)\times(\dot r\,\hat r) +(r\hat r)\times(r\dot\theta\,\hat\theta) \\ &=r\dot r\,(\hat r\times\hat r) +r^2\dot\theta\,(\hat r\times\hat\theta) \\ &=r\dot r\,\mathbf 0 +r^2\dot\theta\,\hat z \\ &=r^2\dot\theta\,\hat z. \end{aligned}

For the right-handed polar basis, \hat r\times\hat r=\mathbf 0 and \hat r\times\hat\theta=\hat z. The chosen orientation has \dot\theta>0, so

h=|\mathbf h|=r^2\dot\theta

Binet equation

Introduce the reciprocal-radius function u(\theta)=1/r(\theta). Since r=1/u, the angular-momentum relation gives

\dot\theta=\frac{h}{r^2}=hu^2

The angle \theta depends on time; u and r depend on \theta. The dependency chain is

t \longrightarrow \theta(t) \longrightarrow u\bigl(\theta(t)\bigr) \longrightarrow r(t)=\frac{1}{u\bigl(\theta(t)\bigr)}

Use dots for derivatives with respect to t and primes for derivatives with respect to \theta:

\dot r=\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm dt}, \qquad u'=\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm d\theta}, \qquad u''=\frac{\mathrm d^2u}{\mathrm d\theta^2}

Apply the chain rule along the full dependency chain:

\begin{aligned} \dot r &=\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm du} \frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm d\theta} \frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm dt} \\ &=(-u^{-2})(u')(\dot\theta) \\ &=(-u^{-2})(u')(hu^2) \\ &=-hu'. \end{aligned}

The factors u^{-2} and u^2 cancel. For the second derivative, h is constant, while u'=u'(\theta(t)) follows the chain t\to\theta(t)\to u'(\theta(t)). Since \mathrm du'/\mathrm d\theta=u'',

\begin{aligned} \ddot r &=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(-hu') \\ &=-h\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} \left[u'\bigl(\theta(t)\bigr)\right] \\ &=-h\frac{\mathrm du'}{\mathrm d\theta} \frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm dt} \\ &=-hu''\dot\theta \\ &=-hu''(hu^2) \\ &=-h^2u^2u''. \end{aligned}

Also,

\begin{aligned} r\dot\theta^2 &=\frac1u(hu^2)^2 =h^2u^3. \end{aligned}

Substitution into Equation \href{#eq:kepler-radial-motion}{\text{(12)}} gives

-h^2u^2u''-h^2u^3 =-\mu_gu^2

Because r>0 and h\ne0, divide by h^2u^2 to obtain the Binet equation:

\boxed{ u''+u=\frac{\mu_g}{h^2} } \qquad{(13)}

Orbit solution

Write the general solution as

u(\theta) =\frac{\mu_g}{h^2} +C\cos(\theta-\omega) =\frac1p\left[1+e\cos(\theta-\omega)\right],

Choose the phase \omega so that C\ge0, and define

p=\frac{h^2}{\mu_g}, \qquad e=pC\ge0

Since r=1/u, the orbit is

\boxed{ r(\theta) =\frac{p}{1+e\cos(\theta-\omega)} } \qquad{(14)}

Conic classification

For e>0, set \nu=\theta-\omega, equivalent to rotating the polar axis by \omega. This true anomaly is measured from periapsis, so \nu=0 at periapsis. Let x=r\cos\nu.

Figure 30 defines the distances used in the focus–directrix classification.

Equation \href{#eq:kepler-conic-orbit}{\text{(14)}} then gives

r+er\cos\nu=p,

or

r=e\left(\frac pe-x\right)

Here r is the distance to the origin. Since p/e-x=r/e>0, the quantity p/e-x is the perpendicular distance to the line x=p/e. Therefore,

\frac{\text{distance to the origin}} {\text{distance to the line }x=p/e} =e

By the focus–directrix definition, the orbit is a conic with the origin at one focus and eccentricity e. It is an ellipse for 0<e<1, a parabola for e=1, and one branch of a hyperbola for e>1. For e=0, Equation \href{#eq:kepler-conic-orbit}{\text{(14)}} gives the circle r=p.

This establishes the conic-section statement in Kepler’s first law. The next exercise identifies which conics are bound.

Energy, eccentricity, and vis-viva

Derive the conserved specific energy, use it to classify the orbit, and obtain the vis-viva equation without assuming circular motion.

Conservation of specific energy

Define the specific mechanical energy of the relative motion:

\varepsilon =\frac12|\dot{\mathbf r}|^2 -\frac{\mu_g}{r} \qquad{(15)}

The signed radial velocity is the radial projection of the full velocity:

\dot r =\hat r\cdot\dot{\mathbf r} =\frac{\mathbf r\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}}{r}

Here \dot r is a scalar; \dot{\mathbf r} is a vector.

Write the squared speed as a dot product and differentiate the kinetic term:

\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} \left(\frac12|\dot{\mathbf r}|^2\right) &=\frac12\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} \left(\dot{\mathbf r}\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}\right) \\ &=\frac12\left( \ddot{\mathbf r}\cdot\dot{\mathbf r} +\dot{\mathbf r}\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r} \right) \\ &=\dot{\mathbf r}\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}. \end{aligned}

For the potential term, apply the chain rule to r=r(t):

\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} \left(-\frac{\mu_g}{r}\right) &=-\mu_g\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(r^{-1}\right) \\ &=-\mu_g\left(-r^{-2}\dot r\right) \\ &=\frac{\mu_g}{r^2}\dot r. \end{aligned}

Adding both derivatives gives

\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm d\varepsilon}{\mathrm dt} &=\dot{\mathbf r}\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r} +\frac{\mu_g}{r^2}\dot r. \end{aligned}

Substitute the relative equation of motion,

\ddot{\mathbf r}=-\frac{\mu_g}{r^3}\mathbf r,

and use the radial-velocity identity in the form

\dot{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf r=r\dot r

Then

\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm d\varepsilon}{\mathrm dt} &=-\frac{\mu_g}{r^3} \dot{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf r +\frac{\mu_g}{r^2}\dot r \\ &=-\frac{\mu_g}{r^3}(r\dot r) +\frac{\mu_g}{r^2}\dot r \\ &=-\frac{\mu_g}{r^2}\dot r +\frac{\mu_g}{r^2}\dot r \\ &=0. \end{aligned}

Hence \varepsilon is conserved.

Energy and eccentricity

Use

\dot r=-hu', \qquad r\dot\theta=\frac hr=hu

The squared relative speed becomes

|\dot{\mathbf r}|^2 =\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2 =h^2\left[(u')^2+u^2\right]

With \nu=\theta-\omega, Equation \href{#eq:kepler-conic-orbit}{\text{(14)}} gives

u=\frac{1+e\cos\nu}{p}, \qquad u'=-\frac{e\sin\nu}{p}, \qquad h^2=\mu_gp

Substituting these expressions into Equation \href{#eq:kepler-specific-energy}{\text{(15)}} gives

\begin{aligned} \varepsilon &=\frac{h^2}{2} \left[(u')^2+u^2\right]-\mu_gu \\ &=\frac{h^2}{2p^2} \left[e^2\sin^2\nu+(1+e\cos\nu)^2\right] -\frac{\mu_g}{p}(1+e\cos\nu) \\ &=\frac{\mu_g}{2p}(e^2-1). \end{aligned}

Equivalently,

\boxed{ e^2 =1+\frac{2\varepsilon h^2}{\mu_g^2} } \qquad{(16)}

Bound-orbit criterion

For 0\le e<1, the denominator in Equation \href{#eq:kepler-conic-orbit}{\text{(14)}} satisfies

1-e \le 1+e\cos\nu \le 1+e,

so r remains finite and positive. For e=1, the denominator approaches zero at \nu=\pi. For e>1, it vanishes when \cos\nu=-1/e. In both cases, the orbit can reach arbitrarily large r. Therefore,

\boxed{ \mathrm{bound\;orbit} \iff e<1 \iff \varepsilon<0 }

A bound, collision-free orbit is therefore an ellipse. This completes Kepler’s first law.

Ellipse parameters

For an ellipse, periapsis and apoapsis occur at \nu=0 and \nu=\pi:

r_p=\frac{p}{1+e}, \qquad r_a=\frac{p}{1-e}

Their sum equals the major-axis length 2a:

\begin{aligned} a &=\frac{r_p+r_a}{2} \\ &=\frac p2 \left(\frac1{1+e}+\frac1{1-e}\right) \\ &=\frac{p}{1-e^2}. \end{aligned}

Therefore,

p=a(1-e^2) \qquad{(17)}

Vis-viva equation

Combine p=a(1-e^2) with \varepsilon=\mu_g(e^2-1)/(2p):

\boxed{ \varepsilon=-\frac{\mu_g}{2a} } \qquad{(18)}

Substitute this energy into the definition of \varepsilon, with v=|\dot{\mathbf r}|:

\frac12v^2-\frac{\mu_g}{r} =-\frac{\mu_g}{2a},

so

\boxed{ v^2 =\mu_g\left(\frac2r-\frac1a\right) } \qquad{(19)}

This is the vis-viva equation for the relative motion. To recover the total mechanical energy in the center-of-mass frame, multiply \varepsilon by the reduced mass

m_{\mathrm{red}}=\frac{Mm}{M+m}

Then

\boxed{ E_{\mathrm{rel}} =m_{\mathrm{red}}\varepsilon =-\frac{GMm}{2a} }

In any other inertial frame, add the constant kinetic energy of the center of mass. This derivation does not use the circular-orbit relation v^2/r=\mu_g/r^2.

Orbital period and Kepler’s third law

Combine ellipse geometry with the constant areal velocity to derive the exact two-body form of Kepler’s third law.

Ellipse geometry

Let c be the center-to-focus distance and b the semi-minor axis. Figure 31 shows the required lengths and the area swept during one period.

The periapsis and apoapsis distances along the major axis are

r_p=a-c, \qquad r_a=a+c

Subtracting these expressions yields

\begin{aligned} c &=\frac{r_a-r_p}{2} \\ &=\frac p2 \left(\frac1{1-e}-\frac1{1+e}\right) \\ &=\frac{pe}{1-e^2} \\ &=ae, \end{aligned}

where the last step uses Equation \href{#eq:kepler-ellipse-p}{\text{(17)}}. Since b^2=a^2-c^2,

\begin{aligned} b^2 &=a^2(1-e^2) \\ &=ap. \end{aligned}

Therefore,

p=\frac{b^2}{a} \qquad{(20)}

Orbital area and period

Scaling the unit disk by a and b along perpendicular axes multiplies its area by ab. Hence the ellipse has area

A_{\mathrm{ellipse}}=\pi ab

During one period T, the relative position sweeps out the entire ellipse. Equation \href{#eq:kepler-area-rate}{\text{(11)}} gives

\pi ab=\frac h2T,

or

T=\frac{2\pi ab}{h}

Kepler’s third law

Use p=h^2/\mu_g with Equation \href{#eq:kepler-ellipse-parameter}{\text{(20)}}:

h^2 =\mu_gp =\mu_g\frac{b^2}{a}

Substitute this result into the period:

\begin{aligned} T^2 &=\frac{4\pi^2a^2b^2}{h^2} \\ &=\frac{4\pi^2a^2b^2} {\mu_gb^2/a} \\ &=\frac{4\pi^2}{\mu_g}a^3. \end{aligned}

Since \mu_g=G(M+m),

\boxed{ T^2 =\frac{4\pi^2}{G(M+m)}a^3 } \qquad{(21)}

This is the exact Newtonian two-body form of Kepler’s third law. For M\gg m, it reduces to

\frac{T^2}{a^3} \approx\frac{4\pi^2}{GM} =\text{constant}

The eccentricity does not appear in the result. For fixed total mass, the orbital period depends only on the semi-major axis and is independent of eccentricity.

Fluid Mechanics

Pressure

Use force balance on a stationary fluid element to derive pressure differences before substituting numerical values.

Consider a horizontal fluid slab of area A and thickness \mathrm dy, with y measured upward. The pressure force from below points upward, while the pressure force from above and the slab’s weight point downward. Figure 32 isolates the slab and the vertical forces used in the balance.

Equilibrium requires

P(y)A-P(y+\mathrm dy)A-\rho gA\,\mathrm dy=0

Divide by A\,\mathrm dy and take the limit \mathrm dy\to0:

\frac{\mathrm dP}{\mathrm dy}=-\rho g

For constant density, integrating from a surface at pressure P_0 to a point a depth h below it gives

P=P_0+\rho gh

A diver is 10.0\ \mathrm m below the surface of fresh water. Take

\rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}, \qquad g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}, \qquad P_0=1.01\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}

The gauge pressure is

P_{\mathrm{gauge}} =\rho gh =(1000)(9.81)(10.0) =9.81\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}

The absolute pressure is

P_{\mathrm{absolute}} =P_0+P_{\mathrm{gauge}} =1.99\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}

Gauge pressure omits the surface pressure; absolute pressure includes it.

Archimedes’ Principle

Use the volume actually displaced by the object, which need not equal the object’s total volume.

Floating fraction and ballast

A uniform block has volume

V=1.00\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^3}

and density \rho_b=600\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}. It floats in fresh water of density \rho_w=1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}. Find the fraction of the block below the surface and the compact load of negligible volume that makes the block just fully submerged.

For the unloaded floating block, buoyancy balances weight:

\rho_wgV_{\mathrm{sub}}=\rho_bgV

Therefore,

\frac{V_{\mathrm{sub}}}{V} =\frac{\rho_b}{\rho_w} =0.600

Thus 60.0\% of the block is submerged. When the block is just fully submerged, it displaces its full volume. The added load is

\begin{aligned} m_{\mathrm{load}} &=\rho_wV-\rho_bV \\ &=(1000-600)(1.00\times10^{-2}) \\ &=4.00\ \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}

For a homogeneous floating object, the submerged volume fraction equals the ratio of object density to fluid density.

Apparent weight and density

A solid object reads 50.0\ \mathrm N on a spring scale in air and 30.0\ \mathrm N when fully submerged in fresh water. Neglect air buoyancy and find the object’s density.

The loss of scale reading is the buoyant force:

F_B=W-T=50.0-30.0=20.0\ \mathrm N

Hence the object’s volume is

V=\frac{F_B}{\rho_wg}

Its mass is m=W/g, so its density can be found without separately evaluating m or V:

\begin{aligned} \rho_{\mathrm{object}} &=\frac{m}{V} \\ &=\rho_w\frac{W}{F_B} \\ &=(1000)\frac{50.0}{20.0} \\ &=2.50\times10^3\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} \end{aligned}

The submerged scale reading is the tension, not the buoyant force.

Fluid Dynamics

Use vorticity to test local fluid-element rotation; straight streamlines do not by themselves imply irrotational flow.

Consider the steady planar shear flow

\vec v=ay\,\hat{\imath}

where a>0 is constant. Its vorticity is

\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega &=\nabla\times\vec v \\ &=\left( \frac{\partial v_y}{\partial x} -\frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y} \right)\hat{k} \\ &=-a\hat{k} \end{aligned}

Therefore the local angular velocity of a fluid element is

\frac{\boldsymbol\omega}{2} =-\frac a2\hat{k}

Figure 33 visualizes this result: higher layers move faster in the +x direction, so a small paddle wheel rotates clockwise as viewed from +z, even though every streamline is straight.

For example, if a=4.0\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}, the paddle wheel’s angular speed is 2.0\ \mathrm{rad/s}. The flow is steady but rotational. Without irrotationality, a common Bernoulli constant across different streamlines is not guaranteed.

Bernoulli’s Equation

Use continuity to relate the section speeds, then apply Bernoulli’s equation between points on the same streamline.

Venturi flow meter

A horizontal Venturi meter carries water of density \rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}. The wide section has diameter D_1=4.0\ \mathrm{cm}, the throat has diameter D_2=2.0\ \mathrm{cm}, and the pressure taps in Figure 34 measure

P_1-P_2=7.5\ \mathrm{kPa}

The area ratio follows from the diameter ratio:

\frac{A_1}{A_2} =\left(\frac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^2 =4

Continuity gives

A_1v_1=A_2v_2, \qquad v_2=4v_1

Because the meter is horizontal, the gravitational terms cancel. Bernoulli’s equation gives

P_1-P_2 =\frac12\rho\left(v_2^2-v_1^2\right) =\frac{15}{2}\rho v_1^2

Therefore,

\begin{aligned} v_1 &=\sqrt{\frac{2(P_1-P_2)}{15\rho}} \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{2(7.5\times10^3)}{15(1000)}} \\ &=1.0\ \mathrm{m/s} \end{aligned}

and

v_2=4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}

The volume flow rate is

\begin{aligned} Q &=A_1v_1 \\ &=\pi(0.020)^2(1.0) \\ &=1.26\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3/s} \\ &=1.26\ \mathrm{L/s} \end{aligned}

The higher speed at the throat is accompanied by lower static pressure. This ideal result neglects viscous losses; real Venturi meters require calibration.

Maximum range of efflux from an open tank

A large tank stands on level ground and is filled with water to height H. A small hole can be made at height z above the ground. Water leaves the hole horizontally. At what height should the hole be made so that the stream strikes the ground as far from the tank as possible? Find the maximum horizontal distance.

Figure 35 shows the tank geometry and the trajectory of the water stream.

Choose point 1 at the free surface and point 2 at the outlet. Both points are exposed to atmospheric pressure, so

P_1=P_2=P_{\mathrm{atm}}

Because the tank is much wider than the outlet, the free-surface speed is negligible: v_1\approx0. Taking the ground as the zero of gravitational potential, Bernoulli’s equation reduces to

\rho gH =\frac12\rho v^2+\rho gz

The vertical distance from the free surface to the hole is H-z, so Torricelli’s law gives

v=\sqrt{2g(H-z)}

The water has zero initial vertical speed and falls a vertical distance z. Its time of flight is therefore

t=\sqrt{\frac{2z}{g}}

The horizontal speed remains v during the fall, so the range is

\begin{aligned} R(z) &=vt \\ &=\sqrt{2g(H-z)}\sqrt{\frac{2z}{g}} \\ &=2\sqrt{z(H-z)} \end{aligned}

For 0\le z\le H, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives

z(H-z) \le\left(\frac{z+(H-z)}{2}\right)^2 =\frac{H^2}{4}

Equality holds when z=H-z, hence

z=\frac H2, \qquad R_{\max}=H

The hole should be halfway between the ground and the free surface. The fluid-mechanics result used here is Torricelli’s law; the optimal height follows from projectile motion and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, rather than from a separate fluid theorem.

Thermodynamics

Temperature

Ideal Gas Law

Thermal Equilibrium

Temperature probes A and B are separately brought into thermal equilibrium with the same calibration block C held at a fixed state. Must the two probes agree?

Yes. By the zeroth law, systems that are each in thermal equilibrium with the same system are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Correctly calibrated probes A and B must therefore indicate the same temperature.

Gas Thermometry

A constant-volume gas thermometer is used to determine an unknown temperature T_2 from the water triple-point reference T_1=273.16\ \mathrm K. Two runs use different amounts of the same gas. In each run, the gas occupies the same fixed volume; P_1 is measured at T_1 and P_2 at T_2:

P_1\;(\mathrm{kPa}) P_2/P_1
50.0 1.3685
100 1.3740

Estimate T_2 while removing the effect of finite gas density.

For an ideal gas at fixed amount and volume, P/T is constant, so one would expect P_2/P_1=T_2/T_1. The measured ratios differ because intermolecular interactions make this relation depend slightly on gas density. At fixed T_1 and volume, a lower P_1 corresponds to a lower density, so extrapolate R(P_1)=P_2/P_1 to P_1=0.

Assuming R(P_1) is linear over the measured range, its slope is

b=\frac{1.3740-1.3685}{100-50.0} =1.10\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kPa^{-1}}

The zero-pressure intercept is

R(0) =1.3685-b(50.0) =1.3630

Therefore,

T_2=T_1R(0)=372.3\ \mathrm K=99.2\,{}^\circ\mathrm C

The zero-density limit removes the leading dependence on gas species. Temperature ratios require the absolute Kelvin scale. Convert to Celsius only after the ratio calculation:

T_{\mathrm K}=T_{\mathrm C}+273.15\ \mathrm K, \qquad \Delta T_{\mathrm K}=\Delta T_{\mathrm C}

Tire Pressure

A car tire has the following data:

  • specified cold gauge pressure: 240\ \mathrm{kPa};
  • initial gauge pressure: 224\ \mathrm{kPa} at 20.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C;
  • overnight temperature: -20.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C;
  • atmospheric pressure: 101.3\ \mathrm{kPa};
  • warning threshold: 75\% of the specified gauge pressure.

Assume the tire volume and amount of gas remain constant. Determine whether the warning activates after the overnight cooling.

The ideal-gas relation at fixed n and V uses absolute pressure:

P_{1,\mathrm{abs}}=224+101.3=325.3\ \mathrm{kPa}

Thus

P_{2,\mathrm{abs}} =P_{1,\mathrm{abs}}\frac{T_2}{T_1} =(325.3)\frac{253.15}{293.15} =280.9\ \mathrm{kPa}

and the new gauge pressure is

P_{2,\mathrm{gauge}}=280.9-101.3=179.6\ \mathrm{kPa}

The pressure drop is

\Delta P=224-179.6=44.4\ \mathrm{kPa}=6.44\ \mathrm{psi}

The assumed threshold is

P_{\mathrm{threshold}}=0.75(240)=180\ \mathrm{kPa}

Using the unrounded pressure, the tire is just below the threshold and the warning activates. This borderline comparison should be made before rounding.

After driving, suppose the gas warms to 35.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C without any leak. The predicted gauge pressure is

P_{3,\mathrm{gauge}} =(325.3)\frac{308.15}{293.15}-101.3 =240.6\ \mathrm{kPa}

The warm tire can appear correctly inflated even though its cold pressure was low. If instead the tire later returns to 20.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C and reads 205\ \mathrm{kPa} gauge, then at the same T and V,

\frac{n_{\mathrm{later}}}{n_{\mathrm{initial}}} =\frac{205+101.3}{224+101.3} =0.942

About 5.84\% of the gas has escaped; temperature alone cannot explain that same-temperature pressure loss.

Expansion

A steel guitar string of vibrating length L=0.648\ \mathrm m and diameter d=0.254\ \mathrm{mm} is tuned to f_0=329.6\ \mathrm{Hz} at 20.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C. Take its density, Young’s modulus, and linear expansion coefficient to be

\rho=7.85\times10^3\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}, \qquad E=200\ \mathrm{GPa}, \qquad \alpha=12.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}

The distance between the supports remains fixed while the string cools to 0.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C. Ignore changes in the guitar body and find the new frequency and pitch change in cents.

Figure 36 contrasts free thermal contraction with the fixed-support constraint.

The cross-sectional area and linear density are

A=\frac{\pi d^2}{4}=5.07\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m^2}, \qquad \mu=\rho A=3.98\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m}

For the fundamental mode, set n=1 in Physics I (8.01): (20),

f_0=\left.f_n\right|_{n=1,\,F_T=F_0}=\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{F_0}{\mu}}

Solving for the initial tension gives

F_0=\mu(2Lf_0)^2=72.6\ \mathrm N

Cooling would produce the free thermal strain \alpha\Delta T. Preventing that contraction increases the tensile stress by -E\alpha\Delta T, so

\Delta F=-EA\alpha\Delta T =-(200\times10^9)(5.07\times10^{-8})(12.0\times10^{-6})(-20.0) =2.43\ \mathrm N

The new frequency is therefore

f_1=f_0\sqrt{\frac{F_0+\Delta F}{F_0}} =(329.6)\sqrt{\frac{75.0}{72.6}} =335.1\ \mathrm{Hz}

One octave is 1200 cents, hence

\Delta c=1200\log_2\frac{f_1}{f_0}=28.5\ \text{cents}

The isolated string becomes sharp because cooling raises its tension. A real instrument can shift differently because the neck, body, and strings all expand and contract.

First Law

Internal Energy

State and Path

A sealed gas completes a cycle and returns to its initial P, V, and T after delivering 2.40\ \mathrm{kJ} of net work. Find the net heat transferred to the gas, and classify internal energy, heat, and work.

A state function is a property determined by the current equilibrium state; its change depends only on the endpoint states. Internal energy U is a state function, so

\Delta U_{\mathrm{cycle}}=0

With work positive when done by the gas, the first law gives

0=Q_{\mathrm{net}}-W_{\mathrm{net}} \implies Q_{\mathrm{net}}=2.40\ \mathrm{kJ}

The gas ends with the same P, V, T, and U, but nonzero heat and work have crossed the boundary. Thus U is a state function, while heat and work are process quantities that depend on the path.

Bicycle Pump

A bicycle pump contains 0.0500\ \mathrm{mol} of air at 20.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C. During a rapid stroke, 60.0\ \mathrm J of work is done on the air and heat transfer is negligible. Model air as a rigid diatomic ideal gas with C_V=5R/2.

With W defined as work done by the gas,

Q=0, \qquad W=-60.0\ \mathrm J

so

\Delta U=Q-W=60.0\ \mathrm J

Since \Delta U=nC_V\Delta T,

\Delta T =\frac{60.0}{(0.0500)(5R/2)} =57.7\ \mathrm K

The idealized final temperature is

T_f=293.15+57.7=350.9\ \mathrm K=77.7\,{}^\circ\mathrm C

A slower stroke would transfer more heat to the cylinder and produce a lower peak temperature.

Heat Capacity

A 0.300\ \mathrm{kg} aluminum pot containing 0.500\ \mathrm{kg} of water starts at 20.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C. A 500\ \mathrm W heater runs for 180\ \mathrm s. Neglect evaporation and heat loss, and use c_{\mathrm{Al}}=900\ \mathrm{J/(kg\,K)} and c_w=4180\ \mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}.

Find the idealized final temperature.

The combined heat capacity is

C=(0.300)(900)+(0.500)(4180) =2360\ \mathrm{J/K}

The heater supplies

Q=Pt=(500)(180)=90.0\ \mathrm{kJ}

Therefore,

\Delta T=\frac{Q}{C}=38.1\ \mathrm K, \qquad T_f=58.1\,{}^\circ\mathrm C

An observed lower temperature measures energy lost to the room, stove, and evaporation.

Phase Change

A 0.300\ \mathrm{kg} drink at 25.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C receives 0.100\ \mathrm{kg} of ice at -10.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C. Use c_w=4180\ \mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}, c_i=2100\ \mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}, and L_f=334\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}. Assume an insulated cup.

Determine the equilibrium temperature and whether any ice remains.

Cooling the drink to 0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C releases

Q_{\mathrm{drink}}=(0.300)(4180)(25.0)=31.35\ \mathrm{kJ}

Warming the ice to 0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C requires

Q_{\mathrm{warm}}=(0.100)(2100)(10.0)=2.10\ \mathrm{kJ}

The remaining 29.25\ \mathrm{kJ} melts

m_{\mathrm{melt}} =\frac{29.25\ \mathrm{kJ}}{334\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}} =0.0876\ \mathrm{kg}

Thus 12.4\ \mathrm g of ice remains and the equilibrium temperature is 0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C. Assuming all the ice melts before checking the energy balance would give an impossible result.

PV Work

An ideal gas moves from

(P_1,V_1)=(200\ \mathrm{kPa},10.0\ \mathrm L)

to

(P_2,V_2)=(100\ \mathrm{kPa},20.0\ \mathrm L)

Figure 37 shows the two paths between the same endpoint states.

Because P_1V_1=P_2V_2, the endpoint temperatures are equal and \Delta U=0. Along a quasistatic isothermal path,

W_A=P_1V_1\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1} =(2.00\ \mathrm{kJ})\ln2 =1.39\ \mathrm{kJ}

For path B, first cool at fixed V_1 from 200 to 100\ \mathrm{kPa}, then expand at 100\ \mathrm{kPa} to V_2. Only the second leg does boundary work:

W_B=P_2(V_2-V_1) =(100\ \mathrm{kPa})(10.0\ \mathrm L) =1.00\ \mathrm{kJ}

Figure 38 compares the signed areas under the two paths.

For both paths Q=W because \Delta U=0, but the heat and work differ even though the endpoint states are identical.

Heat Transfer

Conduction

Derive the equivalent thermal resistance for layers in series and for independent heat-flow paths in parallel. For each uniform layer, use

R_i=\frac{L_i}{k_iA_i}, \qquad \dot Q_i=\frac{\Delta T_i}{R_i}

For layers in series, the same steady rate \dot Q passes through every layer. The total temperature difference is
