\Delta T=\sum_i\Delta T_i =\sum_i\dot Q R_i =\dot Q\sum_iR_i

Since \dot Q=\Delta T/R_{\mathrm{eq}},

\boxed{R_{\mathrm{eq}}=\sum_iR_i} \qquad\text{(series)}

For parallel paths, every path has the same temperature difference while the rates add:

\dot Q=\sum_i\dot Q_i =\sum_i\frac{\Delta T}{R_i} =\Delta T\sum_i\frac1{R_i}

Therefore,

\boxed{\frac1{R_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\sum_i\frac1{R_i}} \qquad\text{(parallel)}

For a building material, the quoted R-value is resistance per unit area:

R_i''=\frac{L_i}{k_i}, \qquad R_i=\frac{R_i''}{A_i}

The electrical-resistance analogy works because temperature difference plays the role of voltage and heat-transfer rate plays the role of current.

Convection

Model steady heat transfer through a house wall from the indoor air to the outdoor air. Use the following assumptions:

  • Heat flow is steady and one-dimensional within each wall region.
  • Indoor convection, the solid layers, and outdoor convection act in series.
  • The insulated field and metal-framing bridge are independent parallel paths; the bridge replaces only the insulation layer in its path.
  • Material properties are constant. Contact resistance, lateral heat spreading, and vapor diffusion are neglected. Surface condensation is diagnosed by comparing the indoor surface temperature with the dew point.

The layer data are

Layer L\;(\mathrm m) k\;(\mathrm{W/(m\,K)})
Gypsum 0.0130 0.170
Insulation 0.0900 0.0400
Metal bridge 0.0900 1.50
Brick 0.100 0.720
  • Convection coefficients: h_i=8.00\ \mathrm{W/(m^2K)} indoors and h_o=25.0\ \mathrm{W/(m^2K)} outdoors.
  • Boundary temperatures: T_i=21.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C and T_o=-20.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C.
  • Indoor relative humidity: 50\% (T_{\mathrm{dew}}=10.2\,{}^\circ\mathrm C).
  • Wall areas: 90.0\% insulated field and 10.0\% metal bridge, with total area A=120\ \mathrm{m^2}.

Determine:

  1. the heat flux and indoor surface temperature through the insulated field;
  2. whether surface condensation occurs in the field or at the bridge, and the critical outdoor temperature for condensation at the bridge;
  3. the total wall heat loss and the error caused by ignoring the bridge.

Figure 39 shows the insulated field and the parallel metal-framing path.

For either path, the series resistance, heat flux, and indoor surface temperature are

R''=\frac1{h_i}+\sum_j\frac{L_j}{k_j}+\frac1{h_o}, \qquad q''=\frac{T_i-T_o}{R''}, \qquad T_{s,i}=T_i-\frac{q''}{h_i}

Start with the insulated field. Its thermal resistance per unit area is

\begin{aligned} R''_{\mathrm{field}} &=\frac1{h_i}+\frac{0.0130}{0.170} +\frac{0.0900}{0.0400}+\frac{0.100}{0.720}+\frac1{h_o} \\ &=2.63\ \mathrm{m^2K/W} \end{aligned}

The heat flux and indoor surface temperature are

q''_{\mathrm{field}} =\frac{21.0-(-20.0)}{2.63} =15.6\ \mathrm{W/m^2}

T_{s,i,\mathrm{field}} =T_i-\frac{q''_{\mathrm{field}}}{h_i} =21.0-\frac{15.6}{8.00} =19.1\,{}^\circ\mathrm C

Since 19.1\,{}^\circ\mathrm C>10.2\,{}^\circ\mathrm C, the insulated-field surface remains dry.

For the thermal-bridge path, replace only the insulation resistance by the metal-bridge resistance:

R''_{\mathrm{bridge}} =\frac1{h_i}+\frac{0.0130}{0.170} +\frac{0.0900}{1.50}+\frac{0.100}{0.720}+\frac1{h_o} =0.440\ \mathrm{m^2K/W}

Figure 40 shows two parallel paths, each containing series resistances.

At the bridge,

q''_{\mathrm{bridge}} =\frac{41.0}{0.440} =93.1\ \mathrm{W/m^2}

T_{s,i,\mathrm{bridge}} =21.0-\frac{93.1}{8.00} =9.36\,{}^\circ\mathrm C

Since 9.36\,{}^\circ\mathrm C<10.2\,{}^\circ\mathrm C, condensation occurs at the bridge even though the insulated field remains dry.

At the condensation threshold, set T_{s,i,\mathrm{bridge}}=T_{\mathrm{dew}} and solve for the outdoor temperature:

\begin{aligned} T_{\mathrm{dew}} &=T_i-\frac{T_i-T_{o,\mathrm{crit}}}{h_iR''_{\mathrm{bridge}}} \\ \implies\quad T_{o,\mathrm{crit}} &=T_i-(T_i-T_{\mathrm{dew}})h_iR''_{\mathrm{bridge}} \\ &=21.0-(21.0-10.2)(8.00)(0.440) \\ &=-17.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C \end{aligned}

Finally, the two wall regions act in parallel. Their area-weighted transmittance is

U=\frac{0.900}{R''_{\mathrm{field}}} +\frac{0.100}{R''_{\mathrm{bridge}}} =0.569\ \mathrm{W/(m^2K)}

and the heat loss is

\dot Q=UA(T_i-T_o) =(0.569)(120)(41.0) =2.80\ \mathrm{kW}

Ignoring the bridge would predict only

\dot Q_{\mathrm{field\ only}} =\frac{120(41.0)}{2.63} =1.87\ \mathrm{kW}

The 10\% bridge area raises the modeled wall loss by about 49.9\%. The surface-temperature test diagnoses surface condensation; predicting moisture inside the wall would additionally require vapor diffusion and material vapor resistance.

Radiation

Model a small satellite in deep space as isothermal and in steady radiative equilibrium. The conditions are:

  • Sun-facing projected area: A_p=1.00\ \mathrm{m^2}.
  • Total thermal-radiating area: A_e=6.00\ \mathrm{m^2}.
  • Solar absorptivity: \alpha=0.600; the satellite absorbs this fraction of the incident solar power.
  • Infrared emissivity: \varepsilon=0.800; the satellite emits this fraction of the blackbody power at the same temperature.
  • Solar flux: S=1361\ \mathrm{W/m^2}.
  • Earth radiation, internal power, and conduction through supports are neglected.

Find the satellite’s radiative equilibrium temperature.

Figure 41 distinguishes the Sun-facing projected area from the total emitting area.

Absorbed solar power is

P_{\mathrm{abs}}=\alpha SA_p

and emitted thermal radiation is

P_{\mathrm{emit}}=\varepsilon\sigma A_eT^4

Here \sigma=5.670\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W/(m^2K^4)} is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant.

At radiative equilibrium, the satellite’s energy is constant, so P_{\mathrm{abs}}=P_{\mathrm{emit}} and

T =\left(\frac{\alpha SA_p}{\varepsilon\sigma A_e}\right)^{1/4} =\left[ \frac{(0.600)(1361)(1.00)} {(0.800)(5.670\times10^{-8})(6.00)} \right]^{1/4} =234\ \mathrm K

Thus T\simeq-39\,{}^\circ\mathrm C. The fourth-root dependence means that doubling absorbed power does not double temperature; it raises T only by 2^{1/4}.

Kinetic Theory

Pressure

A 40.0\ \mathrm L compressed-gas cylinder contains ideal gas at 250\ \mathrm{kPa} absolute pressure and 300\ \mathrm K. Find the number of molecules and the average normal force on a 0.200\ \mathrm{m^2} patch of its wall.

The molecular count is

N=\frac{PV}{k_{\mathrm B}T} =\frac{(250\times10^3)(0.0400)}{(1.380649\times10^{-23})(300)} =2.41\times10^{24}

Pressure is momentum transfer per unit area, so the wall patch experiences

F=PA=(250\times10^3)(0.200)=50.0\ \mathrm{kN}

The cylinder does not accelerate because comparable pressure forces act in all directions; the wall material carries the resulting tensile stress.

Equipartition

Compare one mole of monatomic helium and one mole of rigid diatomic nitrogen at 300\ \mathrm K, with nitrogen vibration frozen out. Equipartition gives

U_{\mathrm{He}}=\frac32RT=3.74\ \mathrm{kJ}

and

U_{\mathrm{N_2}}=\frac52RT=6.24\ \mathrm{kJ}

At constant volume, raising each gas by 100\ \mathrm K requires

Q_{\mathrm{He}}=\frac32R(100)=1.25\ \mathrm{kJ}

Q_{\mathrm{N_2}}=\frac52R(100)=2.08\ \mathrm{kJ}

Nitrogen stores additional energy in rotational motion, so the same energy input produces a smaller temperature rise.

Molar Heat Capacity

One mole of rigid diatomic ideal gas receives 1.00\ \mathrm{kJ} of heat. Compare heating at constant volume with heating at constant pressure, using

C_V=\frac52R, \qquad C_P=\frac72R

At constant volume,

\Delta T_V=\frac{1000}{(5/2)R}=48.1\ \mathrm K

At constant pressure,

\Delta T_P=\frac{1000}{(7/2)R}=34.4\ \mathrm K

The constant-pressure expansion work is

W=nR\Delta T_P=286\ \mathrm J

The remaining 714\ \mathrm J raises internal energy. At constant volume all 1.00\ \mathrm{kJ} raises internal energy, which explains the larger temperature increase.

Adiabatic Process

Air in a bicycle pump begins at P_1=101\ \mathrm{kPa}, T_1=293\ \mathrm K, and volume V_1. It is compressed rapidly and reversibly to V_2=V_1/5. Treat air as ideal with \gamma=1.40.

Find the final temperature and pressure.

For a reversible adiabatic process,

T_2=T_1\left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{\gamma-1} =(293)(5)^{0.40} =558\ \mathrm K

and

P_2=P_1\left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^\gamma =(101\ \mathrm{kPa})(5)^{1.40} =0.961\ \mathrm{MPa}

These high values are an adiabatic upper-limit model. A real pump loses heat, has valve dead volume, and is not perfectly reversible.

Ideal-Gas Processes

One mole of monatomic ideal gas follows the clockwise rectangular cycle

\begin{aligned} A(100\ \mathrm{kPa},10.0\ \mathrm L) &\longrightarrow B(300\ \mathrm{kPa},10.0\ \mathrm L) \\ &\longrightarrow C(300\ \mathrm{kPa},30.0\ \mathrm L) \\ &\longrightarrow D(100\ \mathrm{kPa},30.0\ \mathrm L) \\ &\longrightarrow A \end{aligned}

Find W, \Delta U, and Q on each leg, then find the cycle efficiency.

Figure 42 fixes the path direction on the PV plane.

For a monatomic ideal gas, U=3PV/2. The work, internal-energy change, and heat on each leg are

Leg W\;(\mathrm{kJ}) \Delta U\;(\mathrm{kJ}) Q=\Delta U+W\;(\mathrm{kJ})
A\to B 0 3.00 3.00
B\to C 6.00 9.00 15.0
C\to D 0 -9.00 -9.00
D\to A -2.00 -3.00 -5.00

The net work equals the enclosed PV area:

W_{\mathrm{net}} =(300-100)\ \mathrm{kPa}\,(30.0-10.0)\ \mathrm L =4.00\ \mathrm{kJ}

Heat enters on the first two legs, so

Q_{\mathrm{in}}=3.00+15.0=18.0\ \mathrm{kJ}

and the cycle efficiency is

\eta=\frac{W_{\mathrm{net}}}{Q_{\mathrm{in}}}=0.222

Speed Distribution

At T=293\ \mathrm K, find the most probable, mean, and root-mean-square speeds of nitrogen molecules. Take

M=28.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/mol}

Using k_{\mathrm B}/m=R/M, the most probable speed is

v_{\mathrm{mp}} =\sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}} =417\ \mathrm{m/s}

The mean speed is

\langle v\rangle =\sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}} =471\ \mathrm{m/s}

and the root-mean-square speed is

v_{\mathrm{rms}} =\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} =511\ \mathrm{m/s}

Their ratios do not depend on temperature or molecular mass:

v_{\mathrm{mp}}:\langle v\rangle:v_{\mathrm{rms}} =\sqrt2:\sqrt{\frac8\pi}:\sqrt3 =1:1.13:1.22

Thus v_{\mathrm{mp}}<\langle v\rangle<v_{\mathrm{rms}}. The high-speed tail pulls the mean above the distribution peak, and squaring the speed gives that tail still more weight in v_{\mathrm{rms}}.

Second Law

Heat Engines

Otto Cycle

An ideal Otto cycle models a spark-ignition engine with four internally reversible processes:

  1. 1\to2: adiabatic compression from V_1 to V_2.
  2. 2\to3: isochoric heat addition.
  3. 3\to4: adiabatic expansion from V_2 to V_1.
  4. 4\to1: isochoric heat rejection.

Figure 43 shows the four processes on a schematic PV plane.

Let r=V_1/V_2>1 be the compression ratio. Because the two heat-transfer steps occur at constant volume,

Q_h=nC_V(T_3-T_2), \qquad Q_c=nC_V(T_4-T_1)

The efficiency is therefore

\eta_{\mathrm O} =1-\frac{Q_c}{Q_h} =1-\frac{T_4-T_1}{T_3-T_2}

Apply TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant} to the two adiabatic processes:

\frac{T_2}{T_1}=r^{\gamma-1}, \qquad \frac{T_3}{T_4}=r^{\gamma-1}

Thus

T_4-T_1 =\frac{T_3}{r^{\gamma-1}}-\frac{T_2}{r^{\gamma-1}} =\frac{T_3-T_2}{r^{\gamma-1}}

Substitution gives the Otto-cycle efficiency:

\boxed{\eta_{\mathrm O}=1-\frac1{r^{\gamma-1}}}

This is not a Carnot-cycle derivation: it uses the Otto cycle’s two adiabatic and two isochoric processes. For the same lowest and highest temperatures T_1 and T_3, T_2<T_3 gives

\eta_{\mathrm O}=1-\frac{T_1}{T_2} <1-\frac{T_1}{T_3} =\eta_{\mathrm C}

The Carnot efficiency remains the upper bound because its heat transfers are reversible and isothermal.

Power Plant and River Thermal Pollution

Model a thermal power plant operating steadily with once-through river cooling. Use the following conditions:

  • Electric power output: \dot W=500\ \mathrm{MW}.
  • Overall thermal efficiency: \eta=38.0\%.
  • Effective reservoir temperatures: T_h=550\,{}^\circ\mathrm C and T_c=25.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C.
  • Cooling-water properties: c_p=4.18\ \mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)} and \rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.
  • Cooling-stream temperature rise: 10.0\ \mathrm K.
  • Maximum river bulk-temperature rise after mixing: 2.00\ \mathrm K.
  • All rejected heat enters the cooling water; evaporative cooling, heat loss to air, and thermal storage are neglected.

Determine:

  1. the heat-input rate \dot Q_h;
  2. the rejected-heat rate \dot Q_c;
  3. the Carnot efficiency upper bound and the fraction of that bound reached by the plant;
  4. the required cooling-water mass and volume flow rates;
  5. the minimum total river flow rate after mixing.

Figure 44 defines the energy and cooling-water flows used in the balance.

From \eta=W/Q_h,

\dot Q_h=\frac{500\ \mathrm{MW}}{0.380}=1.32\ \mathrm{GW}

Energy conservation gives

\dot Q_c=\dot Q_h-\dot W =1.316\ \mathrm{GW}-0.500\ \mathrm{GW} =0.816\ \mathrm{GW}

The reservoir temperatures are

T_h=823.15\ \mathrm K, \qquad T_c=298.15\ \mathrm K

so the Carnot limit is

\eta_{\mathrm C}=1-\frac{T_c}{T_h} =1-\frac{298.15}{823.15} =0.638

The plant reaches only

\frac{\eta}{\eta_{\mathrm C}} =\frac{0.380}{0.638} =0.596

of the ideal reversible efficiency. For a 10.0\ \mathrm K rise in the cooling stream,

\dot m =\frac{\dot Q_c}{c_p\Delta T} =\frac{8.16\times10^8}{(4180)(10.0)} =1.95\times10^4\ \mathrm{kg/s}

and therefore

\dot V=\frac{\dot m}{\rho}=19.5\ \mathrm{m^3/s}

If the warmed discharge mixes uniformly with the river and the allowed bulk rise is only 2.00\ \mathrm K, the total receiving flow must satisfy

\dot V_{\mathrm{river}} \geq\frac{\dot Q_c}{\rho c_p(2.00\ \mathrm K)} =97.6\ \mathrm{m^3/s}

The environmental burden follows from the rejected heat, not merely the electrical output. The river-flow estimate assumes no evaporative cooling, heat loss to air, thermal storage, or incomplete mixing.

Refrigerators

Residential Heat Pump
Data

The Daikin Europe technical table and EU energy label give the following data for the Perfera FTXM35A5V1B / RXM35A5V1B air-to-air heat pump:

Quantity Value
Heating capacity, minimum/nominal/maximum 0.80/4.00/5.50\ \mathrm{kW}
Nominal COP 4.55
Average-climate design load P_{\mathrm{design}} 2.50\ \mathrm{kW}
Average-climate SCOP 5.20
Average-climate annual electricity consumption 673\ \mathrm{kWh/a}
Declared heating capacity at -10.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C 2.50\ \mathrm{kW}

Here COP is a single-condition ratio, whereas SCOP is the seasonal ratio from the EU temperature-bin calculation. The design load is a reference load used for that seasonal rating, not electrical input or nominal output.

Assumptions

Use the following exercise assumptions:

  • The 4.00\ \mathrm{kW} capacity applies at T_{\mathrm{out}}=7.00\,{}^\circ\mathrm C.
  • Model capacity as linear through (7.00\,{}^\circ\mathrm C,4.00\ \mathrm{kW}) and (-10.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C,2.50\ \mathrm{kW}). Interpolate for the balance point and 5.00\,{}^\circ\mathrm C; extrapolate to -15.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C.
  • The home has T_{\mathrm{in}}=20.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C and H=0.100\ \mathrm{kW/K}.
  • Resistance backup heat has \mathrm{COP}=1, and electricity costs 0.300\ \mathrm{EUR/kWh}.
  • The running compressor draws P_{\mathrm{el,nom}}. At partial load it cycles with d=\dot Q_{\mathrm{load}}/\dot Q_{\mathrm{capacity}}. Ignore startup, cycling, standby, and distribution losses.
  • Defrost power is 0 at 5.00\,{}^\circ\mathrm C and averages 0.100\ \mathrm{kW} at -15.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C. Capacity is net heat output after defrost. Each temperature lasts 24.0\ \mathrm h.
Questions

Determine:

  1. the nominal electrical input power;
  2. the seasonal useful heat represented by the EU label and its annual electricity cost;
  3. the building load and required backup heat at 7.00\,{}^\circ\mathrm C and -10.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C;
  4. the balance-point temperature under the interpolation model;
  5. the modeled COP and daily electricity cost at 5.00\,{}^\circ\mathrm C and -15.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C.
Capacity Diagram

Figure 45 compares the two published capacity points, their linear interpolation, and the modeled building load.

Nominal and Seasonal Performance

At the nominal condition, the electrical input follows from the definition of COP:

P_{\mathrm{el,nom}} =\frac{\dot Q_{\mathrm{nom}}}{\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{nom}}} =\frac{4.00}{4.55} =0.879\ \mathrm{kW}

The seasonal useful heat represented by the label is

Q_{\mathrm{season}} =\mathrm{SCOP}\,E_{\mathrm{season}} =(5.20)(673\ \mathrm{kWh}) =3.50\ \mathrm{MWh}

and the corresponding electricity cost is

\text{cost}=(673\ \mathrm{kWh})(0.300\ \mathrm{EUR/kWh}) =202\ \mathrm{EUR}

SCOP is a seasonal quantity and cannot be substituted for a single-temperature COP.

Load and Balance Point

The steady building load is

\dot Q_{\mathrm{load}}=H(T_{\mathrm{in}}-T_{\mathrm{out}})

At the two capacity points,

T_{\mathrm{out}} \dot Q_{\mathrm{load}} \dot Q_{\mathrm{capacity}} \dot Q_{\mathrm{backup}}
7.00\,{}^\circ\mathrm C 1.30\ \mathrm{kW} 4.00\ \mathrm{kW} 0
-10.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C 3.00\ \mathrm{kW} 2.50\ \mathrm{kW} 0.50\ \mathrm{kW}

At 7.00\,{}^\circ\mathrm C, the variable-speed unit can reduce its output to meet the load. At -10.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C, the modeled home requires 0.50\ \mathrm{kW} of resistance backup heat.

Under the stated interpolation assumption, the available capacity is

\dot Q_{\mathrm{capacity}}(T) =2.50+\frac{4.00-2.50}{7.00-(-10.0)}(T+10.0)

Setting this equal to the building load gives

\begin{aligned} 2.50+\frac{1.50}{17}(T_{\mathrm{balance}}+10.0) &=0.100(20.0-T_{\mathrm{balance}}) \\ \implies T_{\mathrm{balance}} &=-7.34\,{}^\circ\mathrm C \end{aligned}

Below this temperature, the interpolated capacity is smaller than the modeled building load.

Mild Day

At 5.00\,{}^\circ\mathrm C, the capacity model and building model give

\dot Q_{\mathrm{capacity}}(5.00) =2.50+\frac{1.50}{17}(5.00+10.0) =3.82\ \mathrm{kW}

\dot Q_{\mathrm{load}}(5.00) =0.100(20.0-5.00) =1.50\ \mathrm{kW}

The unit therefore cycles with duty factor

d_5=\frac{1.50}{3.82}=0.392

With no modeled defrost at this temperature, its operating COP and daily electricity cost are

\mathrm{COP}_5=\frac{3.82}{0.879}=4.35

E_{\mathrm{day},5} =(0.392)(0.879\ \mathrm{kW})(24.0\ \mathrm h) =8.28\ \mathrm{kWh}

\mathrm{cost}_5=(8.28)(0.300)=2.48\ \mathrm{EUR/day}

Cold Day

At -15.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C, extrapolation of the capacity model gives

\dot Q_{\mathrm{capacity}}(-15.0) =2.50+\frac{1.50}{17}(-15.0+10.0) =2.06\ \mathrm{kW}

The building needs 3.50\ \mathrm{kW}, so the heat pump runs continuously and resistance backup supplies

\dot Q_{\mathrm{backup}} =0.100[20.0-(-15.0)]-2.06 =1.44\ \mathrm{kW}

Including the average-equivalent defrost input, the heat-pump COP is

\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{HP},-15}=\frac{2.06}{0.879+0.100}=2.10

The whole-system COP, daily electricity use, and cost are

\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{system},-15}=\frac{3.50}{0.879+0.100+1.44}=1.45

E_{\mathrm{day},-15} =(0.879+0.100+1.44\ \mathrm{kW})(24.0\ \mathrm h) =58.1\ \mathrm{kWh}

\mathrm{cost}_{-15}=(58.1)(0.300)=17.4\ \mathrm{EUR/day}

Outdoor temperature Heat-pump COP Whole-system COP Daily electricity Daily cost
5.00\,{}^\circ\mathrm C 4.35 4.35 8.28\ \mathrm{kWh} 2.48\ \mathrm{EUR}
-15.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C 2.10 1.45 58.1\ \mathrm{kWh} 17.4\ \mathrm{EUR}

The sharp cold-day increase comes from three effects in the model: greater building heat loss, lower available heat-pump capacity, and the combined defrost and resistance-backup electricity.

Winter EV Range

An electric car has:

  • mild-temperature usable energy 72.0\ \mathrm{kWh};
  • traction consumption 18.0\ \mathrm{kWh/100\,km} at 90.0\ \mathrm{km/h};
  • 90.0\% of its mild-temperature usable energy at -15.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C;
  • cabin heating load 4.00\ \mathrm{kW} at -15.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C.

Ignore stops and other accessory loads. Determine:

  1. the mild-temperature range;
  2. the cold-weather range with resistance heating and heat pumps at COP 2.00 and 3.00;
  3. the minimum heater COP required for 320\ \mathrm{km} of range.

At mild temperature, with no cabin heat required, the idealized range is

R_{\mathrm{mild}} =\frac{72.0}{18.0}\,(100\ \mathrm{km}) =400\ \mathrm{km}

In the cold, the usable energy and traction power are

E_{\mathrm{cold}}=0.900(72.0)=64.8\ \mathrm{kWh}

P_{\mathrm{traction}} =\left(18.0\ \frac{\mathrm{kWh}}{100\ \mathrm{km}}\right) \left(90.0\ \frac{\mathrm{km}}{\mathrm h}\right) =16.2\ \mathrm{kW}

For heater COP C, the total electrical power and range are

P_{\mathrm{total}}=16.2+\frac{4.00}{C}, \qquad R=\frac{E_{\mathrm{cold}}}{P_{\mathrm{total}}}(90.0\ \mathrm{km/h})

Therefore,

Cabin heater P_{\mathrm{total}} R
Resistance, C=1.00 20.2\ \mathrm{kW} 289\ \mathrm{km}
Heat pump, C=2.00 18.2\ \mathrm{kW} 320\ \mathrm{km}
Heat pump, C=3.00 17.5\ \mathrm{kW} 333\ \mathrm{km}

The cold battery alone limits the range to

R_{\mathrm{cold,no\ heat}}=0.900(400)=360\ \mathrm{km}

Covering 320\ \mathrm{km} takes

t=\frac{320}{90.0}=3.56\ \mathrm h

so the maximum average electrical power is

P_{\max}=\frac{64.8}{3.56}=18.2\ \mathrm{kW}

The cabin system can draw at most

P_{\mathrm{cabin,max}}=18.2-16.2=2.03\ \mathrm{kW}

and must achieve

\mathrm{COP}_{\min}=\frac{4.00}{2.03}=1.98

Battery derating and cabin heating reduce range separately.

Statements

Show that the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements are equivalent by demonstrating that a violation of either statement would violate the other.

First suppose a Kelvin–Planck-violating engine absorbs energy W from one hot reservoir and converts it entirely to work. Use that work to drive an ordinary refrigerator that removes Q_c from a cold reservoir and rejects Q_c+W to the hot reservoir. The work transfers cancel. The hot reservoir has the net gain

(Q_c+W)-W=Q_c

while the cold reservoir loses Q_c. The sole net effect is transfer from cold to hot without work, which violates the Clausius statement.

Conversely, suppose a Clausius-violating device transfers Q_c from cold to hot without work. Couple it to an ordinary engine that absorbs Q_h from the hot reservoir, rejects Q_c to the cold reservoir, and produces

W=Q_h-Q_c

The two Q_c transfers cancel. The sole net effect is removal of W from one hot reservoir and its complete conversion to work, which violates the Kelvin–Planck statement. Each violation implies the other, so the statements are equivalent.

Reversibility

One mole of ideal gas expands isothermally at 300\ \mathrm K from 10.0\ \mathrm L to 20.0\ \mathrm L. Compare a reversible expansion with an irreversible expansion against the constant external pressure equal to the gas’s final pressure.

Both processes connect the same equilibrium states. The comparison shows how the path changes the work delivered by the gas.

Figure 46 compares the boundary-work areas for the reversible and constant-external-pressure processes.

The reversible work is

W_{\mathrm{rev}} =nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1} =(8.314)(300)\ln2 =1.729\ \mathrm{kJ}

For the irreversible path,

P_{\mathrm{ext}}=\frac{nRT}{V_2}=124.7\ \mathrm{kPa}

and

W_{\mathrm{irr}} =P_{\mathrm{ext}}(V_2-V_1) =(124.7\ \mathrm{kPa})(10.0\ \mathrm L) =1.247\ \mathrm{kJ}

The internal-energy change is zero for both paths because the initial and final temperatures are the same. Work, however, depends on the path. The reversible gas pushes against the largest possible external pressure at each volume, so the area under its PV curve is larger:

W_{\mathrm{rev}}-W_{\mathrm{irr}} =1.729-1.247 =0.482\ \mathrm{kJ}

In the constant-pressure process, the initial pressure difference is finite, so the gas expands without passing through a sequence of equilibrium states. Reversing the piston motion would not restore both the gas and its surroundings without other changes. Under the same endpoint and environmental constraints, the reversible expansion therefore delivers the maximum work. The Isothermal Expansion exercise relates the missing work to entropy generation.

Carnot Cycle

One mole of ideal diatomic gas with \gamma=1.40 operates a Carnot engine between T_h=600\ \mathrm K and T_c=300\ \mathrm K. At state A, V_A=10.0\ \mathrm L. The hot isothermal expansion doubles the volume to V_B=20.0\ \mathrm L. Find V_C, V_D, the heat transfers, work, and efficiency.

Figure 47 shows the two isotherms and two adiabats; the drawing is not to scale.

For the adiabatic expansion B\to C,

T_hV_B^{\gamma-1}=T_cV_C^{\gamma-1}

so

V_C =V_B\left(\frac{T_h}{T_c}\right)^{1/(\gamma-1)} =(20.0\ \mathrm L)(2)^{2.5} =113\ \mathrm L

The two isothermal volume ratios are equal, hence

\frac{V_B}{V_A}=\frac{V_C}{V_D}=2 \implies V_D=56.6\ \mathrm L

The hot and cold isothermal heat-transfer magnitudes are

Q_h=nRT_h\ln\frac{V_B}{V_A} =(8.314)(600)\ln2 =3.46\ \mathrm{kJ}

Q_c=nRT_c\ln\frac{V_C}{V_D} =(8.314)(300)\ln2 =1.73\ \mathrm{kJ}

Therefore,

W=Q_h-Q_c=1.73\ \mathrm{kJ}

and

\eta=\frac{W}{Q_h}=0.500=1-\frac{T_c}{T_h}

The large adiabatic volume change follows from the modest temperature ratio raised to 1/(\gamma-1)=2.5.

Entropy

Entropy Change

A 0.350\ \mathrm{kg} cup of coffee with effective specific heat c=4.18\ \mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)} cools from 80.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C to a room at 20.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C. Treat the room as a thermal reservoir and ignore evaporation. The heat released is

Q=mc(T_i-T_0) =(0.350)(4180)(353.15-293.15) =87.8\ \mathrm{kJ}

Entropy is a state function, so the coffee’s entropy change can be calculated along an imagined reversible path between the same states. For a small temperature change, the reversibly transferred heat is \delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}=mc\,\mathrm dT. Because the coffee’s temperature is not constant, entropy must be integrated over that temperature range:

\Delta S_{\mathrm{coffee}} =\int_{T_i}^{T_0}\frac{mc\,\mathrm dT}{T} =mc\ln\frac{T_0}{T_i} =(0.350)(4180)\ln\frac{293.15}{353.15} =-272\ \mathrm{J/K}

The result is negative because the coffee cools and loses entropy. The room, in contrast, remains at the constant temperature T_0, so its entropy change can be calculated directly as Q/T_0.

The room receives Q at the constant reservoir temperature T_0:

\Delta S_{\mathrm{room}} =\frac{Q}{T_0} =\frac{87780}{293.15} =299\ \mathrm{J/K}

Entropy Production

The following two exercises reach the same conclusion. Under the same initial and final states and the same environmental constraints, a reversible process delivers the maximum work. If the environment is a thermal reservoir at uniform temperature T_0, then

W_{\mathrm{lost}} =W_{\mathrm{rev}}-W_{\mathrm{actual}} =T_0S_{\mathrm{gen}}

Energy is conserved; entropy generation measures the loss of the ability to convert energy into work.

Cooling Coffee

Therefore direct cooling produces

S_{\mathrm{gen}} =\Delta S_{\mathrm{coffee}}+\Delta S_{\mathrm{room}} =27.0\ \mathrm{J/K}>0

Energy is conserved, but entropy increases because heat crosses a finite temperature difference.

Now place an ideal reversible engine between the coffee at instantaneous temperature T and the room at T_0. As the coffee releases a small amount of heat, the engine’s Carnot efficiency is 1-T_0/T. The maximum total work is

\begin{aligned} W_{\max} &=mc\int_{T_0}^{T_i}\left(1-\frac{T_0}{T}\right)\mathrm dT \\ &=mc\left[(T_i-T_0)-T_0\ln\frac{T_i}{T_0}\right] \\ &=7.92\ \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}

Only

\frac{W_{\max}}{Q}=0.0902

or 9.02\% of the released thermal energy could ideally become work because the coffee is only moderately hotter than the room. Moreover,

T_0S_{\mathrm{gen}} =(293.15)(27.0\ \mathrm{J/K}) \simeq7.92\ \mathrm{kJ} =W_{\max}

Isothermal Expansion

This example continues the Reversibility exercise above. For either isothermal ideal-gas path, \Delta U=0, so the heat absorbed by the gas equals the work it delivers. Because work depends on the path, the two processes absorb different amounts of heat:

Q_{\mathrm{rev}}=W_{\mathrm{rev}}=1.729\ \mathrm{kJ}, \qquad Q_{\mathrm{irr}}=W_{\mathrm{irr}}=1.247\ \mathrm{kJ}

The reservoir remains at T=300\ \mathrm K and loses the heat absorbed by the gas. Its entropy change is therefore \Delta S_{\mathrm{res}}=-Q_{\mathrm{gas}}/T. For the reversible path,

\Delta S_{\mathrm{res,rev}} =-\frac{Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T} =-\frac{1.729\ \mathrm{kJ}}{300\ \mathrm K} =-5.76\ \mathrm{J/K}

For the constant-pressure path,

\Delta S_{\mathrm{res,irr}} =-\frac{Q_{\mathrm{irr}}}{T} =-\frac{1.247\ \mathrm{kJ}}{300\ \mathrm K} =-4.16\ \mathrm{J/K}

The reservoir loses less entropy in the irreversible process because the gas absorbs less heat. The gas itself has the same entropy change along either path because entropy depends only on the initial and final states:

\Delta S_{\mathrm{gas}}=nR\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}=nR\ln2=5.76\ \mathrm{J/K}

In the reversible process, the gas gains 5.76\ \mathrm{J/K} while the reservoir loses the same amount, so no entropy is generated. In the irreversible process, entropy transferred with heat accounts for only 4.16\ \mathrm{J/K} of the gas’s entropy increase. The rest is generated by the process itself:

S_{\mathrm{gen}} =\Delta S_{\mathrm{gas}}+\Delta S_{\mathrm{res,irr}} =nR\ln2-\frac{Q_{\mathrm{irr}}}{T} =1.61\ \mathrm{J/K}

At the reservoir temperature T=300\ \mathrm K, the lost work is

TS_{\mathrm{gen}} \simeq(300\ \mathrm K)(1.61\ \mathrm{J/K}) \simeq0.482\ \mathrm{kJ} =W_{\mathrm{rev}}-W_{\mathrm{irr}}

Microstates

Twenty distinguishable molecules can independently occupy the left or right half of a box with equal probability. Compare the balanced macrostate with the macrostate in which all molecules lie on one side, including their probability and entropy difference. The total number of microstates is 2^{20}. The macrostate with ten molecules on each side has multiplicity

\Omega_{10,10}=\binom{20}{10}=184756

and probability

P_{10,10}=\frac{184756}{2^{20}}=0.176

The macrostate in which all molecules occupy either one side or the other has only two microstates:

P_{\mathrm{all\ on\ one\ side}} =\frac{2}{2^{20}} =1.91\times10^{-6}

The entropy difference between these two macrostates is

\Delta S =k_{\mathrm B}\ln\frac{184756}{2} =1.58\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{J/K}

For only twenty molecules, fluctuations remain visible. For macroscopic particle numbers, the multiplicity advantage of balanced distributions becomes overwhelming.

Oscillations

Simple Harmonic Motion

Use torque about the pivot to identify simple harmonic motion. Unlike a simple pendulum, the period of a physical pendulum depends on how its mass is distributed.

A rigid body of mass M rotates freely in a vertical plane about a fixed horizontal axis through O. Its center of mass is a distance d from the axis, and its moment of inertia about the axis is I_O. The body is displaced through a small angle \theta_0 from stable equilibrium and released from rest. Find its period, then apply the result to a uniform slender rod of length L and mass M pivoted at one end.

Figure 48 shows the geometry used to calculate the torque about O. Measure \theta from the downward vertical.

Gravity produces the restoring torque

{\tau}_O=-Mgd\sin\theta

Thus the exact equation of motion is

I_O\ddot\theta=-Mgd\sin\theta

For small oscillations, \sin\theta\approx\theta, so

\ddot\theta+\frac{Mgd}{I_O}\theta=0

This is simple harmonic motion with

\omega=\sqrt{\frac{Mgd}{I_O}}, \qquad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I_O}{Mgd}}

The initial conditions \theta(0)=\theta_0 and \dot\theta(0)=0 give

{\theta}(t)=\theta_0\cos\left(\sqrt{\frac{Mgd}{I_O}}\,t\right)

For the uniform rod pivoted at one end, Figure 49 defines the displaced configuration and the stable vertical equilibrium.

Its center of mass and moment of inertia about the pivot are

d=\frac L2, \qquad I_O=I_{\mathrm{cm}}+M\left(\frac L2\right)^2 =\frac{1}{12}ML^2+\frac14ML^2 =\frac13ML^2

Therefore,

\omega_{\mathrm{rod}} =\sqrt{\frac{Mg(L/2)}{ML^2/3}} =\sqrt{\frac{3g}{2L}}

and its small-oscillation period is

\boxed{T_{\mathrm{rod}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2L}{3g}}}

The equivalent simple-pendulum length is

\ell_{\mathrm{eq}} =\frac{I_O}{Md} =\frac{2L}{3}

The formula requires the center of mass, the moment of inertia about the actual pivot axis, and the small-angle approximation.

Waves

Waves on a String

Basics

This exercise distinguishes the motion of a wave from the motion of the material carrying it. A pulse travels to the right along a horizontal string while a painted marker on the string moves only up and down. Explain why this does not require the string material to move horizontally.

The marker follows one fixed material element, whereas the pulse follows the position of a moving feature of the field y(x,t). Neighboring string elements move up and down in sequence, making the pulse shape travel horizontally even though no element travels with it. The wave therefore transports energy, not string material, along the string. Because the material displacement is perpendicular to the direction of propagation, this is a transverse wave.

Traveling Wave

For a traveling wave, separate the motion of the wave pattern from the motion of one material element. Consider

y(x,t)=(3.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m) \sin\left[(4.00\ \mathrm{rad/m})x-(20.0\ \mathrm{rad/s})t+\frac{\pi}{6}\right]

Find its amplitude, wavelength, frequency, speed, and direction of propagation. The following sections use the same wave to compare a fixed material element with a moving crest.

Comparison with y=A\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi) gives

A=3.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m, \qquad k=4.00\ \mathrm{rad/m}, \qquad \omega=20.0\ \mathrm{rad/s}

Hence

\lambda=\frac{2\pi}{k}=1.57\ \mathrm m, \qquad f=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}=3.18\ \mathrm{Hz}, \qquad v=\frac{\omega}{k}=5.00\ \mathrm{m/s}

The minus sign before \omega t shows that the wave pattern travels in the +x direction.

Sine Wave

At a Fixed Position

The string element at x=0 remains at that fixed position. Its initial displacement is

y(0,0)=A\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=1.50\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m

Its transverse velocity follows by differentiating at fixed x:

u_y(0,0) =\left.\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}\right|_{(0,0)} =-A\omega\cos\frac{\pi}{6} =-5.20\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m/s}

Thus the element is moving downward even though the wave travels to the right.

At a Fixed Phase

A crest has phase \pi/2+2\pi n, so

4x-20t+\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{2}+2\pi n \implies x_n(t)=5.00t+\frac{\pi}{12}+\frac{n\pi}{2}

At t=0, the first crest with x\ge0 is therefore at x_0=\pi/12=0.262\ \mathrm m. Its velocity is \mathrm dx_0/\mathrm dt=5.00\ \mathrm{m/s}, while no string element moves horizontally in this transverse-wave model.

Wave Equation for a String

The wave above travels on a string with linear density \mu=8.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/m}. Verify that it satisfies the string wave equation, find the required tension F_T, and determine the new wave speed and angular frequency if the tension is quadrupled while \mu and k remain unchanged.

Direct differentiation gives

\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial t^2}=-\omega^2y=-400y, \qquad v^2\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial x^2} =-v^2k^2y =-(5.00)^2(4.00)^2y =-400y

Thus \partial^2y/\partial t^2=v^2\partial^2y/\partial x^2, as required.

Using the string-wave speed derived in the main note, the required tension is

F_T=\mu v^2 =(8.00\times10^{-3})(5.00)^2 =\boxed{0.200\ \mathrm N}

Quadrupling the tension doubles the speed. Since \omega=vk and k remains fixed,

v'=\sqrt{\frac{4F_T}{\mu}}=2v=\boxed{10.0\ \mathrm{m/s}}, \qquad \omega'=v'k=(10.0)(4.00)=\boxed{40.0\ \mathrm{rad/s}}

Energy and Power

A string has linear density \mu=5.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/m} and tension F_T=45.0\ \mathrm N. A sinusoidal wave of amplitude A=2.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m and frequency f=120\ \mathrm{Hz} travels along it. Find the wave speed, wavelength, energy in one wavelength, and average power. If the amplitude is halved while the tension is quadrupled, with f and \mu unchanged, find the new average power.

The wave speed and wavelength are

v=\sqrt{\frac{F_T}{\mu}} =\sqrt{\frac{45.0}{5.00\times10^{-3}}} =94.9\ \mathrm{m/s}, \qquad \lambda=\frac{v}{f}=0.791\ \mathrm m

With \omega=2\pi f=754\ \mathrm{rad/s}, the energy carried in one wavelength is

E_\lambda =\frac12\mu\omega^2A^2\lambda =\frac12(5.00\times10^{-3})(754)^2(2.00\times10^{-3})^2(0.791) =4.49\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm J

One wavelength passes a fixed point during each period, so the same result for the average power follows either from E_\lambda f or directly from the power formula:

\overline{\mathcal P} =E_\lambda f =\frac12\mu\omega^2A^2v =0.539\ \mathrm W

At fixed f and \mu, \overline{\mathcal P}\propto A^2v\propto A^2\sqrt{F_T}. Therefore,

\frac{\overline{\mathcal P}'}{\overline{\mathcal P}} =\left(\frac{A/2}{A}\right)^2 \sqrt{\frac{4F_T}{F_T}} =\frac12 \implies \boxed{\overline{\mathcal P}'=0.270\ \mathrm W}

Sound Waves

Sound Wave Equation

Homogeneous Fluid

Starting from the bulk-modulus relation between pressure and longitudinal strain, derive the wave equation for a homogeneous fluid and identify its wave speed.

The constitutive relation is

\Delta p=-B\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}

The pressure forces on a slice of equilibrium length \mathrm dx give

F_x =-A_c\frac{\partial\Delta p}{\partial x}\,\mathrm dx =BA_c\frac{\partial^2s}{\partial x^2}\,\mathrm dx

Its mass is \rho A_c\,\mathrm dx, so Newton’s second law gives

\rho A_c\,\mathrm dx\frac{\partial^2s}{\partial t^2} =BA_c\frac{\partial^2s}{\partial x^2}\,\mathrm dx

Therefore,

\boxed{ \frac{\partial^2s}{\partial t^2} =\frac B\rho\frac{\partial^2s}{\partial x^2} }, \qquad \boxed{v=\sqrt{\frac B\rho}}

The bulk modulus supplies the restoring response and density supplies the inertia.

Ideal Gas
Thermal Motion

Express the ideal-gas sound speed directly in terms of the molecular rms speed. Then evaluate both speeds for nitrogen at T=293\ \mathrm K, taking M=28.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/mol} and \gamma=1.40.

Using the kinetic-theory pressure relation Physics I (8.01): (6) and \rho=Nm/V gives

\frac{P_0}{\rho} =\frac{(Nm/3V)\langle v^2\rangle}{Nm/V} =\frac13v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2

The sound-wave speed Physics I (8.01): (17) and the ideal-gas adiabatic bulk modulus Physics I (8.01): (18) give v_{\mathrm{sound}}=\sqrt{B/\rho} and B=\gamma P_0. Therefore,

v_{\mathrm{sound}} =\sqrt{\frac{\gamma P_0}{\rho}} =\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{3}}\,v_{\mathrm{rms}}

For nitrogen,

v_{\mathrm{rms}} =\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} =511\ \mathrm{m/s}

and therefore

v_{\mathrm{sound}} =\sqrt{\frac{1.40}{3}}(511) =349\ \mathrm{m/s}, \qquad \frac{v_{\mathrm{rms}}}{v_{\mathrm{sound}}} =\sqrt{\frac3\gamma}=1.46

The molecular rms speed describes random motion, whereas the sound speed describes the propagation of a collective pressure disturbance. Their fixed ratio does not make them the same motion.

The molecules move faster than the pressure disturbance, but their velocity directions are random. To estimate the resulting net displacement, take the mean free path to be \ell=68.0\ \mathrm{nm}. During t=1.00\ \mathrm{ms}, a molecule undergoes approximately

N\simeq\frac{v_{\mathrm{rms}}t}{\ell} =\frac{(511)(1.00\times10^{-3})}{68.0\times10^{-9}} =7.52\times10^6

collisions. A simple random-walk estimate gives

d_{\mathrm{rms}}\simeq\ell\sqrt N =1.86\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm m =0.186\ \mathrm{mm}

In the same time, sound travels

d_{\mathrm{sound}}=v_{\mathrm{sound}}t=0.349\ \mathrm m

Sound is a collective pressure disturbance passed from molecule to molecule; it does not require one molecule to travel from the source to the listener.

Reference Wave

A plane sinusoidal sound wave travels through dry air at T_K=293\ \mathrm K. Take \gamma=1.40, M=28.97\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/mol}, and \rho=1.20\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}. The wave has frequency f=1.00\ \mathrm{kHz} and sound level \beta=80.0\ \mathrm{dB}. First find the sound speed; the following sections use the same wave to relate displacement, pressure, energy, and intensity.

For an ideal gas, the adiabatic sound speed is

v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT_K}{M}} =\sqrt{\frac{(1.40)(8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)})(293\ \mathrm K)} {28.97\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/mol}}} =343\ \mathrm{m/s}

Sine Sound Wave

Derive the relation between displacement amplitude and pressure amplitude for a right-moving sinusoidal sound wave.

For a right-moving displacement wave

s(x,t)=s_{\max}\cos(kx-\omega t),

the pressure change is

\Delta p =-B\frac{\partial s}{\partial x} =Bk s_{\max}\sin(kx-\omega t)

Using B=\rho v^2 and v=\omega/k gives

\boxed{\Delta p_{\max}=\rho v\omega s_{\max}}

Pressure and fluid velocity are in phase for a right-moving wave, while displacement differs from them by one quarter cycle.

Energy, Power, and Intensity

The sound level determines the intensity:

I=I_0 10^{\beta/10} =(1.00\times10^{-12})10^{80.0/10} =1.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}

Using I=(\Delta p_{\max})^2/(2\rho v) gives

\Delta p_{\max} =\sqrt{2\rho vI} =\sqrt{2(1.20)(343)(1.00\times10^{-4})} =0.287\ \mathrm{Pa}

Using \Delta p_{\max}=\rho v\omega s_{\max} with \omega=2\pi f gives

s_{\max} =\frac{\Delta p_{\max}}{\rho v(2\pi f)} =\frac{0.287}{(1.20)(343)(2\pi)(1.00\times10^3)} =1.11\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm m

The very small displacement is consistent with an audible pressure wave: pressure depends on the spatial compression of the air, not on air elements traveling with the wave.

Sound Doppler Effect

Only velocity components along the sound ray enter the Doppler shift. Apply the formula once for direct sound and once for each source–observer role in a reflection.

1-D Motion

Reflected Wave

A stationary transmitter and receiver are colocated at x=0. The transmitter emits f_0=2.00\ \mathrm{kHz} toward a flat wall to the right. In air where v=340\ \mathrm{m/s}, the reflected signal is received at f_{\mathrm{echo}}=2.25\ \mathrm{kHz}. Treat the reflection as elastic in the wall frame. Determine the wall’s speed and whether it is approaching or receding.

Figure 50 separates the incident and reflected legs, on which the moving wall changes roles.

Suppose the wall approaches the instruments with speed U. For the incident ray, \hat n=\hat i and the wall is an observer with \vec u_O=-U\hat i. It receives

f_1=f_0\frac{v-(-U)}{v}=f_0\frac{v+U}{v}

In the wall frame, reflection preserves this frequency. For the return ray, \hat n=-\hat i and the wall acts as a source with \vec u_S=-U\hat i, so \vec u_S\cdot\hat n=U. The stationary receiver therefore detects

f_{\mathrm{echo}} =f_1\frac{v}{v-U} =f_0\frac{v+U}{v-U}

Let r=f_{\mathrm{echo}}/f_0=2.25/2.00=1.125. Solving for U gives

r=\frac{v+U}{v-U} \implies U=v\frac{r-1}{r+1} =(340)\frac{1.125-1}{1.125+1} =20.0\ \mathrm{m/s}

Because the echo frequency is higher than the transmitted frequency, the wall is approaching. A receding wall would instead produce the factor (v-U)/(v+U)<1.

Motion in Any Direction

A source emits f_S=1.00\ \mathrm{kHz} sound in still air where v=343\ \mathrm{m/s}. From source to observer, the sound ray has direction

\hat n=\frac35\hat i+\frac45\hat j

The source and observer velocities relative to the air are

\vec u_S=(20.0\ \mathrm{m/s})\hat i, \qquad \vec u_O=-(15.0\ \mathrm{m/s})\hat j

Find the observed frequency and compare it with the first-order approximation for speeds small relative to v.

The required projections are

\vec u_S\cdot\hat n=(20.0)\frac35=12.0\ \mathrm{m/s}, \qquad \vec u_O\cdot\hat n=(-15.0)\frac45=-12.0\ \mathrm{m/s}

Therefore,

f_O =f_S\frac{v-\vec u_O\cdot\hat n}{v-\vec u_S\cdot\hat n} =(1.00\times10^3)\frac{343-(-12.0)}{343-12.0} =1.073\times10^3\ \mathrm{Hz}

The source moves toward the observer along the ray, while the observer moves toward the source, so both effects raise the frequency. The first-order result is

f_O \simeq f_S\left[1+ \frac{(\vec u_S-\vec u_O)\cdot\hat n}{v}\right] =(1.00\times10^3)\left(1+\frac{24.0}{343}\right) =1.070\times10^3\ \mathrm{Hz}

The small difference from the exact value comes from neglecting terms of second and higher order in u/v. Velocity perpendicular to \hat n does not contribute to this instantaneous frequency shift.

Supersonic Source

A jet flies horizontally at constant altitude h=5.00\ \mathrm{km}. Its Mach cone has half-angle \theta=30.0^\circ, and the sound speed is v=343\ \mathrm{m/s}. Find the Mach number, jet speed, and the time between the jet passing directly overhead and an observer hearing the sonic boom.

The cone relation gives

\mathcal M=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}=2.00, \qquad v_S=\mathcal Mv=686\ \mathrm{m/s}

When the cone reaches the observer, the jet is a horizontal distance x ahead. The cone geometry gives

\operatorname{tan}\theta=\frac{h}{x} \implies x=h\cot\theta =(5.00\ \mathrm{km})\cot30.0^\circ =8.66\ \mathrm{km}

Thus the delay after the overhead passage is

\Delta t=\frac{x}{v_S} =\frac{8.66\times10^3}{686} =12.6\ \mathrm s

This delay is set by the moving cone geometry; it is not simply h/v. If the source were subsonic, v_S<v would require \sin\theta=v/v_S>1, so no real Mach cone could form.

Superposition

Interference

Phasor Addition

Two coherent waves in the same medium have the same k and \omega:

y_1=(3.00\ \mathrm{mm})\sin\vartheta, \qquad y_2=(4.00\ \mathrm{mm})\sin(\vartheta+120^\circ), \qquad \vartheta=kx-\omega t

Find the amplitude and phase of the resultant wave. Then compare its intensity with the sum of the two individual intensities.

Expanding the shifted sine gives

y_1+y_2 =(A_1+A_2\cos\delta)\sin\vartheta +A_2\sin\delta\cos\vartheta

For A_1=3.00\ \mathrm{mm}, A_2=4.00\ \mathrm{mm}, and \delta=120^\circ,

A_1+A_2\cos\delta=1.00\ \mathrm{mm}, \qquad A_2\sin\delta=2\sqrt3\ \mathrm{mm}

Writing the sum as A_R\sin(\vartheta+\phi) and matching coefficients gives

A_R =\sqrt{(1.00)^2+(2\sqrt3)^2}\ \mathrm{mm} =\sqrt{13}\ \mathrm{mm} =3.61\ \mathrm{mm}

and

\phi =\operatorname{atan2}(2\sqrt3,1) =73.9^\circ

For waves with the same frequency in the same medium, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. Therefore,

\frac{I_R}{I_1+I_2} =\frac{A_R^2}{A_1^2+A_2^2} =\frac{13}{3^2+4^2} =0.520

The negative cross term 2A_1A_2\cos120^\circ makes this partially destructive interference. The fields add first; intensity must be calculated from the resultant field rather than added independently.

Active Noise Cancellation

An active-noise-canceling headphone measures a sinusoidal noise pressure

p_n(t)=p_0\cos\omega t

and attempts to produce an equal-amplitude opposite pressure at the ear. After calibration, suppose an uncorrected delay \Delta t remains, so the anti-noise arriving at the ear is

p_a(t)=-p_0\cos\left[\omega(t-\Delta t)\right]

Find the residual sound level for \Delta t=50.0\ \mu\mathrm s at 500\ \mathrm{Hz}, 1.00\ \mathrm{kHz}, and 4.00\ \mathrm{kHz}. Then find the maximum delay error and equivalent path-length error that still permit at least 20.0\ \mathrm{dB} cancellation at 1.00\ \mathrm{kHz} and 4.00\ \mathrm{kHz}. Take the speed of sound as 343\ \mathrm{m/s}.

Figure 51 shows the direct noise path and the delayed anti-noise path through the controller.

Superposition gives

p_n+p_a =p_0\left\{\cos\omega t-\cos[\omega(t-\Delta t)]\right\}

Using the cosine-difference identity, the residual pressure amplitude relative to the original noise is

\frac{p_{\mathrm{res}}}{p_0} =2\left|\sin\frac{\omega\Delta t}{2}\right| =2|\sin(\pi f\Delta t)|

Figure 52 shows geometrically how the delay leaves a nonzero residual pressure.

The sound-level change relative to the original noise is

\Delta\beta =20\log_{10}\frac{p_{\mathrm{res}}}{p_0}

For the stated delay,

f p_{\mathrm{res}}/p_0 \Delta\beta
500\ \mathrm{Hz} 0.157 -16.1\ \mathrm{dB}
1.00\ \mathrm{kHz} 0.313 -10.1\ \mathrm{dB}
4.00\ \mathrm{kHz} 1.176 +1.41\ \mathrm{dB}

At 4.00\ \mathrm{kHz} the delayed anti-noise makes the result louder than the original noise. To obtain at least 20.0\ \mathrm{dB} cancellation,

20\log_{10}\frac{p_{\mathrm{res}}}{p_0}\le-20 \implies \frac{p_{\mathrm{res}}}{p_0}\le0.100

Therefore,

2|\sin(\pi f\Delta t_{\max})|=0.100 \implies \Delta t_{\max}=\frac{\arcsin(0.0500)}{\pi f}

At 1.00\ \mathrm{kHz},

\Delta t_{\max}=15.9\ \mu\mathrm s, \qquad \Delta\ell_{\max}=v\Delta t_{\max}=5.46\ \mathrm{mm}

At 4.00\ \mathrm{kHz},

\Delta t_{\max}=3.98\ \mu\mathrm s, \qquad \Delta\ell_{\max}=1.37\ \mathrm{mm}

The allowed timing and path errors shrink as 1/f. This is why feedforward active cancellation is much easier for steady low-frequency engine noise than for short-wavelength high-frequency sound.

Beats

A 440\ \mathrm{Hz} tuning fork and an unknown fork produce six beats per second. Adding a small amount of wax to the unknown fork lowers its frequency by less than 6\ \mathrm{Hz}, after which two beats per second are heard. Find the unknown fork’s original frequency and the frequency change caused by the wax.

Initially,

|f_u-440\ \mathrm{Hz}|=6\ \mathrm{Hz} \implies f_u=434\ \mathrm{Hz}\ \text{or}\ 446\ \mathrm{Hz}

If f_u=434\ \mathrm{Hz}, lowering it would increase its separation from 440\ \mathrm{Hz}, so the beat frequency could not fall from 6 to 2\ \mathrm{Hz}. Thus the unknown fork was initially above the standard:

\boxed{f_u=446\ \mathrm{Hz}}

Because the wax lowers the frequency by less than 6\ \mathrm{Hz}, the shifted frequency remains above 440\ \mathrm{Hz}. Hence

f_u'-440\ \mathrm{Hz}=2\ \mathrm{Hz} \implies f_u'=442\ \mathrm{Hz}

The wax lowers the unknown frequency by

\Delta f=f_u'-f_u=442-446=-4\ \mathrm{Hz}

The absolute value in f_{\mathrm{beat}}=|f_1-f_2| creates two candidates; the direction of a controlled frequency change is what selects the physical one.

Standing Waves

Formation and Properties

Two waves of amplitude A=2.00\ \mathrm{mm}, wavelength \lambda=0.800\ \mathrm m, and frequency f=50.0\ \mathrm{Hz} travel in opposite directions on the same string:

y_R=A\sin(kx-\omega t), \qquad y_L=A\sin(kx+\omega t)

Find the resultant wave, the node and antinode positions, the local amplitude at x=0.100\ \mathrm m, and the net average energy transport.

Their superposition is

y=y_R+y_L=2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)

Nodes occur where \sin(kx)=0:

x_n^{(\mathrm{node})} =\frac{n\lambda}{2} =n(0.400\ \mathrm m)

Antinodes occur halfway between adjacent nodes:

x_n^{(\mathrm{antinode})} =\frac{(2n+1)\lambda}{4} =(2n+1)(0.200\ \mathrm m)

At x=0.100\ \mathrm m, the local oscillation amplitude is

A_{\mathrm{local}} =2A\left|\sin\frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}\right| =(4.00\ \mathrm{mm})\sin\frac\pi4 =2.83\ \mathrm{mm}

The two traveling waves carry equal average powers in opposite directions, so the standing wave has zero net average energy transport even though energy moves locally during each cycle.

Normal Modes

Theory

Use separation of variables and the two fixed-end boundary conditions to derive the allowed wavenumbers, wavelengths, and frequencies of a string of length L. Seek a separated solution

y(x,t)=X(x)T(t)

of

\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial t^2} =v^2\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial x^2}

Separation gives

\frac{T''}{v^2T}=\frac{X''}{X}=-k^2

and hence

X''+k^2X=0, \qquad T''+\omega^2T=0, \qquad \omega=vk

The spatial solution is

X=C\sin(kx)+D\cos(kx)

The boundary condition X(0)=0 gives D=0, while X(L)=0 requires

\sin(kL)=0 \implies k_n=\frac{n\pi}{L}, \qquad n=1,2,3,\ldots

Therefore,

\lambda_n=\frac{2L}{n}, \qquad f_n=\frac{nv}{2L}

The boundary conditions convert the continuous range of traveling-wave frequencies into a discrete normal-mode spectrum.

Case Study

A string of length L=1.20\ \mathrm m is fixed at both ends. Its linear density is \mu=6.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/m} and its tension is F_T=54.0\ \mathrm N. A resonance is observed at 197.6\ \mathrm{Hz}. Determine the mode number, wavelength, node and antinode positions, and phase relation between neighboring loops. Find the tension required to raise this same mode to 220\ \mathrm{Hz}.

The traveling-wave speed and fundamental frequency are

v=\sqrt{\frac{F_T}{\mu}} =\sqrt{\frac{54.0}{6.00\times10^{-3}}} =94.9\ \mathrm{m/s}, \qquad f_1=\frac{v}{2L}=39.5\ \mathrm{Hz}

For a string fixed at both ends, f_n=nf_1. Thus

n=\frac{197.6}{39.5}=5.00

The resonance is the fifth normal mode, and five half-wavelengths fit along the string:

\lambda_5=\frac{2L}{5}=0.480\ \mathrm m

Its nodes are separated by \lambda_5/2=0.240\ \mathrm m:

x_j=\frac{jL}{5}=j(0.240\ \mathrm m), \qquad j=0,1,\ldots,5

The antinodes lie halfway between adjacent nodes:

x_j=\frac{(2j+1)L}{10}=(2j+1)(0.120\ \mathrm m), \qquad j=0,1,\ldots,4

All points within one interval between nodes oscillate in phase. Neighboring intervals have opposite signs in the spatial mode and therefore differ in phase by \pi.

For fixed L, \mu, and mode number,

f_n=\frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{F_T}{\mu}} \implies F_T'=\mu\left(\frac{2Lf_n'}{n}\right)^2

The required tension is

F_T' =(6.00\times10^{-3}) \left[\frac{2(1.20)(220)}{5}\right]^2 =66.9\ \mathrm N

Changing the tension changes the traveling-wave speed and every allowed frequency, but the fifth-mode node pattern remains fixed by n and L.

Other Systems
Air Columns

A uniform air column of length L supports longitudinal displacement s(x,t)=X(x)\cos\omega t. Derive the nonzero natural frequencies for tubes whose ends are both open, both closed, or one closed and one open. Identify the pressure behavior at each type of end. Then find the first three resonances of each frequency family for L=0.850\ \mathrm m and v=340\ \mathrm{m/s}.

The spatial part of a normal mode satisfies

X''+k^2X=0, \qquad X(x)=C\sin kx+D\cos kx, \qquad f=\frac{vk}{2\pi}

At a closed end, the air cannot move longitudinally, so X=0. At an open end, the pressure change is approximately zero. Since \Delta p=-B\,\partial s/\partial x, an open end requires X'=0.

For an open–open tube, X'(0)=0 gives C=0. The condition at x=L then gives

X'(L)=-Dk\sin kL=0 \implies k_nL=n\pi, \qquad n=1,2,3,\ldots

For a closed–closed tube, X(0)=0 gives D=0, and

X(L)=C\sin kL=0 \implies k_nL=n\pi, \qquad n=1,2,3,\ldots

Thus both same-type boundary conditions give

\boxed{f_n=\frac{nv}{2L}}, \qquad n=1,2,3,\ldots

For a tube closed at x=0 and open at x=L, X(0)=0 again gives D=0. The open-end condition gives

X'(L)=Ck\cos kL=0 \implies k_nL=\frac{(2n-1)\pi}{2}

Hence

\boxed{f_n=\frac{(2n-1)v}{4L}}, \qquad n=1,2,3,\ldots

The mixed tube has only odd multiples of its fundamental because an odd number of quarter-wavelengths must fit between a displacement node and a displacement antinode.

For the stated tube,

\frac{v}{2L}=\frac{340}{2(0.850)}=200\ \mathrm{Hz}, \qquad \frac{v}{4L}=100\ \mathrm{Hz}

Therefore, the first three resonances are

\begin{aligned} f_n&=200,\ 400,\ 600\ \mathrm{Hz} &&\text{open--open or closed--closed}, \\ f_n&=100,\ 300,\ 500\ \mathrm{Hz} &&\text{closed--open} \end{aligned}

An open end is a displacement antinode and pressure node. A closed end is a displacement node and, for these ideal modes, a pressure antinode.

Rods

A slender uniform rod has cross-sectional area A, Young’s modulus E, mass density \rho_s, and longitudinal displacement u(x,t). Derive its wave equation and wave speed from a short rod element. Then obtain the nonzero mode families for fixed and stress-free ends.

For a small longitudinal strain, the stress is

\sigma=E\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}

The net longitudinal force on an element from x to x+\mathrm dx is

F_x =A\left[\sigma(x+\mathrm dx,t)-\sigma(x,t)\right] \simeq EA\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}\,\mathrm dx

Its mass is \rho_sA\,\mathrm dx, so Newton’s second law gives

\rho_sA\,\mathrm dx\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial t^2} =EA\,\mathrm dx\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2} \implies \boxed{ \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial t^2} =\frac{E}{\rho_s}\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2} }, \qquad \boxed{c_L=\sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho_s}}}

For u=X(x)T(t), the spatial factor is

X(x)=C\sin kx+D\cos kx, \qquad f=\frac{c_Lk}{2\pi}

A fixed end requires X=0. At a stress-free end, \sigma=EX'=0, so X'=0. Applying the same condition at both ends gives k_nL=n\pi for every nonzero mode, whether the rod is fixed–fixed or free–free. Therefore,

\boxed{f_n=\frac{nc_L}{2L}}, \qquad n=1,2,3,\ldots

For a rod fixed at x=0 and free at x=L, X(0)=0 gives D=0, while

X'(L)=Ck\cos kL=0 \implies k_nL=\frac{(2n-1)\pi}{2}

Thus

\boxed{f_n=\frac{(2n-1)c_L}{4L}}, \qquad n=1,2,3,\ldots

As a numerical example, take an aluminum rod with L=1.50\ \mathrm m, E=70.0\ \mathrm{GPa}, and \rho_s=2.70\times10^3\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}. Its longitudinal wave speed is

c_L =\sqrt{\frac{70.0\times10^9}{2.70\times10^3}} =5.09\times10^3\ \mathrm{m/s}

If it is fixed–free, its first two resonances are

f_1=\frac{c_L}{4L}=849\ \mathrm{Hz}, \qquad f_2=\frac{3c_L}{4L}=2.55\times10^3\ \mathrm{Hz}

If the same rod is free–free, its lowest nonzero resonance is

f_1=\frac{c_L}{2L}=1.70\times10^3\ \mathrm{Hz}

The free–free rod also permits k=0 with X=\text{constant} and \omega=0. This is rigid translation, not an oscillatory elastic mode.

Membranes

A rectangular membrane of side lengths L_x and L_y is fixed along all four edges and obeys

\frac{\partial^2z}{\partial t^2} =c_m^2\left( \frac{\partial^2z}{\partial x^2} +\frac{\partial^2z}{\partial y^2} \right)

Derive its normal modes by separation of variables. Then take L_x=0.600\ \mathrm m, L_y=0.400\ \mathrm m, and c_m=120\ \mathrm{m/s}, and find f_{11}, f_{21}, and f_{12}. Identify the internal nodal line of the (2,1) mode and explain the degeneracy that appears when the membrane is square.

Let z(x,y,t)=X(x)Y(y)T(t). Substitution and division by c_m^2XYT give

\frac{T''}{c_m^2T} =\frac{X''}{X}+\frac{Y''}{Y} =-(k_x^2+k_y^2)

The separated spatial equations are

X''+k_x^2X=0, \qquad Y''+k_y^2Y=0

The fixed edges require

X(0)=X(L_x)=0, \qquad Y(0)=Y(L_y)=0

Nonzero solutions therefore have

k_x=\frac{m\pi}{L_x}, \qquad k_y=\frac{n\pi}{L_y}, \qquad m,n=1,2,3,\ldots

Thus the spatial modes and frequencies are

\boxed{ X_{mn}(x,y) =\sin\left(\frac{m\pi x}{L_x}\right) \sin\left(\frac{n\pi y}{L_y}\right) }

and

\omega_{mn} =c_m\sqrt{k_x^2+k_y^2} \implies \boxed{ f_{mn} =\frac{c_m}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{L_x}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{n}{L_y}\right)^2} }

For the rectangular membrane,

\begin{aligned} f_{11} &=60\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{0.600}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{1}{0.400}\right)^2} =180\ \mathrm{Hz}, \\ f_{21} &=60\sqrt{\left(\frac{2}{0.600}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{1}{0.400}\right)^2} =250\ \mathrm{Hz}, \\ f_{12} &=60\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{0.600}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{2}{0.400}\right)^2} =316\ \mathrm{Hz} \end{aligned}

For the (2,1) mode, the interior zero of \sin(2\pi x/L_x) occurs at

x=\frac{L_x}{2}=0.300\ \mathrm m

so the membrane has one internal nodal line parallel to the y axis. If L_x=L_y=L, then

f_{mn}=\frac{c_m}{2L}\sqrt{m^2+n^2}=f_{nm}

Hence (m,n) and (n,m), such as (1,2) and (2,1), are distinct mode shapes with the same frequency. Unequal side lengths generally remove this degeneracy.

Room Modes

A rectangular listening room has dimensions

L_x=5.00\ \mathrm m, \qquad L_y=4.00\ \mathrm m, \qquad L_z=2.60\ \mathrm m

Treat the walls as rigid and take the sound speed as 343\ \mathrm{m/s}. Find the first low-frequency room modes and use the lowest axial mode to explain how subwoofer and listener positions create a bass peak or null.

Figure 53 shows the pressure signs, center nodal plane, and the two listening positions used below.

Rigid walls require zero normal air velocity, so the pressure modes have the form

p_{n_xn_yn_z}(x,y,z) \propto \cos\frac{n_x\pi x}{L_x} \cos\frac{n_y\pi y}{L_y} \cos\frac{n_z\pi z}{L_z}

with n_x,n_y,n_z=0,1,2,\ldots, not all zero. Their frequencies are

f_{n_xn_yn_z} =\frac v2 \sqrt{ \left(\frac{n_x}{L_x}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{n_y}{L_y}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{n_z}{L_z}\right)^2 }

The first several modes are

(n_x,n_y,n_z) Type f
(1,0,0) x-axial 34.3\ \mathrm{Hz}
(0,1,0) y-axial 42.9\ \mathrm{Hz}
(1,1,0) Tangential 54.9\ \mathrm{Hz}
(0,0,1) z-axial 66.0\ \mathrm{Hz}
(2,0,0) x-axial 68.6\ \mathrm{Hz}

For the (1,0,0) mode, the pressure factor along the room is

X(x)=\cos\frac{\pi x}{L_x}

At the front wall, quarter point, and center,

X(0)=1, \qquad X(1.25\ \mathrm m)=\frac1{\sqrt2}, \qquad X(2.50\ \mathrm m)=0

A subwoofer against the front wall couples strongly to the 34.3\ \mathrm{Hz} mode. A listener at the room center lies on its pressure node and hears a deep null, whereas a listener near the quarter point samples about 70.7\% of the mode’s maximum pressure amplitude. For this one mode, putting the source on the center plane would suppress its excitation because the same cosine factor vanishes there.

Equalization cannot fill an ideal geometric null: increasing source power raises pressure elsewhere while the mode remains zero on its nodal plane. Multiple subwoofers and off-symmetry listening positions address multiple modes.
